standards.applicability: Primarily banking institutions offering Islamic financial services: fully fledged Islamic commercial banks, Islamic investment banks/companies, Islamic banking subsidiaries of conventional banks, Islamic windows (branches/divisions/units) of conventional banks, and other institutions determined by the supervisory authority; risk-weighting methodology may also apply to Sharī`ah-compliant assets held by non-self-contained windows or other institutions (para 9). Applies on a fully consolidated basis at holding-company level within a group/sub-group of IIFS, or on a solo basis, or both, as determined by the supervisor; not intended for consolidated application to groups containing non-IIFS entities; application should be commensurate with nature, size and complexity (para 10). Islamic insurance (Takāful) institutions and Islamic collective investment schemes are excluded (title; IIFS acronym definition). Explicitly applicable to Islamic investment banks for the leverage ratio (para 92). Does not cover advanced approaches (IRB, AMA), which remain subject to supervisory discretion (para 17).
standards.structure: Six sections plus Definitions and Appendices A-G (para 15). Section I: Introduction (background paras 1-7; objectives para 8; scope paras 9-10; implementation date para 11; specificities of Islamic financial instruments paras 12-13; structure paras 14-18). Section II: Regulatory Capital (2.1 components of capital incl. CET1/AT1/T2, PSIA-PER-IRR treatment, adjustments/deductions, transition, paras 19-32; 2.2 capital conservation buffer paras 33-53; 2.3 countercyclical buffer paras 54-72; 2.4 leverage ratio paras 73-94; 2.5 Islamic window operations paras 95-104; 2.6 D-SIBs paras 105-122). Section III: Principles for Minimum Capital Requirements (3.1 credit risk incl. ECAI-based claims, off-balance sheet, profit-sharing exposures, preferential RWs, past due, CRM, collateral, haircuts, maturity mismatch, ECAI recognition, paras 123-207; 3.2 market risk paras 208-245; 3.3 operational risk incl. Sharī`ah non-compliance risk paras 246-270; 3.4 PSIA, smoothing, DCR, CAR calculation and alpha paras 271-287). Section IV: Capital Requirements for Islamic Financing and Investment Assets — nine contracts each with stage tables (4.1 Murābahah/MPO paras 289-312; 4.2 CMT paras 313-322; 4.3 Salam paras 323-338; 4.4 Istisnā` paras 339-380; 4.5 Ijārah and IMB paras 381-400; 4.6 Mushārakah and diminishing Mushārakah paras 401-411; 4.7 Muḍārabah paras 412-422; 4.8 Qarḍ paras 423-431; 4.9 Wakālah paras 432-444). Section V: Sukūk and Securitisation (paras 445-536). Section VI: Real Estate Activities (paras 537-566). Appendix A: capital ratio formulas; Appendix B: CCB operational guidelines; Appendix C: Current Exposure Method; Appendix D: Sukūk vs bonds vs shares; Appendices E-F: supervisory slotting criteria; Appendix G: D-SIB factors.
key_points: The Standard combines and revises IFSB-2 (2005) and IFSB-7 (2009) into a single revised capital adequacy standard, further enhanced with features of GN-1, GN-2, GN-3 and GN-4; footnote 5 states the issuance 'is not meant to replace any of these publications' (i.e. the Guidance Notes) (paras 7, 14; fn 5)

Total eligible capital = Tier 1 (CET1 + AT1, 'going concern') + Tier 2 ('gone concern'); minima at all times: CET1 4.5% of RWA, Tier 1 6.0%, total capital 8.0%; plus conservation and countercyclical buffers and D-SIB surcharge where applicable (paras 20-22)

AT1 may consist of Mushārakah Sukūk on the whole business of the bank whose holders fully share risks with shareholders; perpetual, no step-ups, callable only after five years with supervisory approval; general-obligation Muḍārabah Sukūk are in fact Mushārakah Sukūk since the Rabb al-Māl is not liable for general liabilities (para 27; fn 12)

T2 instruments may be Muḍārabah or Wakālah Sukūk convertible into common equity at the point of non-viability with trigger and conversion ratio specified to avoid gharar; minimum original maturity five years; general provisions in T2 capped at 1.25% of credit RWA (paras 28-29; fn 14)

PSIA are not part of capital; all of the IRR and the IAH portion of the PER belong to the equity of investment account holders; any PER portion in the IIFS's reserves is also excluded because PER smooths payouts rather than covering losses (para 30)

CET1 deductions include goodwill/intangibles, DTAs relying on future profitability, treasury shares, pension fund net assets, securitisation gains (retained residual equity risk-weighted 1250%), reciprocal cross-holdings, and investments >10% in banking/financial/Takāful entities via the corresponding deduction approach; zakat obligations must be recognised and disclosed once the IIFS has operated at least 12 months (para 31)

Transition: 8% total capital from 1 January 2014; 4.5% CET1 and 6% Tier 1 from 1 January 2015; regulatory deductions, including amounts above the aggregate 15% limit for significant investments in financial institutions, fully deducted from CET1 by 1 January 2018 (para 32)

Capital conservation buffer of 2.5% RWA in CET1 gives a 7.0% CET1 target; capital conservation ratios: CET1 4.5-5.125% conserve 100% of profits, >5.125-5.75% 80%, >5.75-6.375% 60%, >6.375-7.0% 40%, >7% 0%; phased in from 0.625% on 1 January 2016 rising 0.625%/year to 2.5% on 1 January 2019; 'profits' exclude the share payable to PSIA and are after zakat and PER transfers (paras 36, 40, 44, 51)

Countercyclical buffer of 0-2.5% of RWA wholly in CET1 (higher permitted domestically; reciprocity capped at 2.5%), announced up to 12 months ahead, phased in 2016-2019; Appendix B: buffer add-on is 0 when the credit-to-GDP gap < L=2%, rises linearly to VBmax=2.5% at H=10%, trend computed with a one-sided Hodrick-Prescott filter with lambda 400,000 (paras 68-69, 72; fn 30; Appendix B para 4)

Leverage ratio = Tier 1 capital ÷ total exposure ≥ 3%, calculated as the average of monthly ratios over the quarter, implemented from 1 January 2014; off-balance sheet items 100% CCF (10% for unconditionally cancellable commitments); UPSIA-funded assets included in exposure multiplied by the applicable alpha; RPSIA excluded unless a source of DCR (paras 81, 86-87, 93)

Islamic windows: supervisors may require separate window capital and CAR or consolidated treatment at parent level; a window 'should in principle be required to have separate capital, as this is a Sharī`ah requirement'; window operational risk charge calculated separately for Islamic and conventional operations (paras 97-101; fn 39; para 250)

D-SIBs identified by size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity (Appendix G) must hold HLA of indicatively 0.5%-3.5% CET1 of RWA, applicable from January 2016, plus recovery plans and intensified supervision (paras 111, 117, 121-122; Appendix G)

Standardised credit RWs: sovereigns 0/20/50/100/150% (unrated 100%); MDBs including the IDB group and ICIEC 0%; banks Option 1/2a/2b (2b floor 20% for ≤3-month domestic-currency claims); corporates 20/50/100/150% (unrated 100%); short-term claims 20/50/100/150%; where two ECAI ratings map to different RWs the higher applies (paras 125-127)

CCFs: commitments ≤1 year 20%, >1 year 50%, unconditionally cancellable 0%; collateralised and insured Murābahah import/export LCs 20%; performance/bid bonds and warranties 50%; direct credit substitutes and Sharī`ah-compliant repo alternatives 100%; OTC Sharī`ah-compliant hedging uses the Current Exposure Method (mark-to-market plus add-ons of 0.0-1.5% profit-rate, 1.0-7.5% currency, 10-15% other by tenor) (paras 130-134; Appendix C para 3)

Mushārakah/Muḍārabah equity exposures in the banking book: simple RW method 300% (listed) / 400% (other), with 300% allowed at supervisory discretion for Mushārakah or where funds are withdrawable within a maximum of five working days; supervisory slotting method 90/110/135/270% (Strong/Good/Satisfactory/Weak), including a fixed 20% RW add-on for potential decline in net asset value (paras 142-145)

Preferential RWs: regulatory retail 75% (aggregate receivables per counterparty ≤ US$500,000; diversification e.g. 0.2% cap per counterpart); residential real estate 35% (receivables ≤50% of market value, professional valuation within one year); commercial real estate 100%, or 50% in exceptional circumstances (incl. CRE losses ≤0.5% test); past due >90 days: 150% (specific provisions <20%), 100% (≥20%, or ≥50% with discretion to reduce to 50%), RRE-secured 100% reducible to 50%; other assets 100%, cash items in collection 20% (paras 158-165)

CRM: Hamish Jiddiyah eligible only with a binding PP/PL (fully refundable, hence ineligible, if non-binding); Urbūn, third-party guarantees (min rating A- for corporates), pledged assets (Rahn/Kafālah), leased assets as quasi-collateral, and on-balance-sheet netting are eligible; simple approach substitutes collateral RW subject to a 20% floor (0% for cash/deposit/0%-sovereign collateral discounted 20%); comprehensive approach E* = max[0, E×(1+He) − C×(1−Hc−Hfx)] with supervisory haircuts 0-25% (physical assets ≥30%, FX add-on 8%); maturity-mismatched CRM recognised only if ≥1 year, adjusted Pa = P×(t−0.25)/(T−0.25) (paras 172-198; fn 63)

Market risk: equity positions 8% specific + 8% general; Sukūk specific risk 0% (government) to 0.25/1.00/1.60% (investment grade, by residual maturity ≤6m/6-24m/>24m), 8% (BB+ to B-), 12% (below B-), 8% unrated; general market risk by maturity method (RWs 0.00-6.00% over 13 time bands) or duration method (three zones, vertical and horizontal disallowances 40/30/30%, 40% adjacent, 100% zones 1-3); FX (including gold and silver, which fall under FX risk per Sharī`ah spot-exchange rules) 8% on overall net position; commodities: maturity ladder 1.5% spread per band + 0.6% carry + 15% net, or simplified 15% net + 3% gross; inventory 15%; Istisnā` WIP 8% (unbilled WIP without parallel Istisnā` attracts an additional 1.6% market charge) (paras 222-244; fn 74)

Operational risk: BIA charge = 15% (alpha) of average positive annual gross income over three years; TSA betas by business line 18% (corporate finance, trading & sales, payment & settlement), 15% (commercial banking, agency services), 12% (retail banking, asset management, retail brokerage); ASA substitutes 0.035 × outstanding financing for retail/commercial banking, with 15% for aggregated retail+commercial and 18% for aggregated other six lines; gross income excludes the share attributable to IAH; Sharī`ah non-compliance risk (failure of the Sharī`ah governance mechanism, non-recognition of income, Muḍārib fiduciary liability) is included within operational risk (paras 246-260)

CAR formulas (Appendix A): standard formula = eligible capital ÷ {total RWA (credit+market) + operational risk − RWA funded by PSIA}; supervisory discretion formula additionally deducts RWA funded by restricted PSIA, (1−α) × RWA funded by unrestricted PSIA, and α × RWA funded by PER and IRR of unrestricted PSIA; alpha (the DCR-driven proportion of UPSIA-funded RWA included in the denominator) is set by supervisory discretion, ranging from near 0 (investment-like) to 1 (deposit-like), per the GN-4 methodology (paras 278, 284-287; Appendix A)

Contract stage capital (sale-based): Murābahah/non-binding MPO — asset on balance sheet 15% market charge (187.5% RW), receivable at obligor RW (100% unrated); binding MPO — credit exposure = acquisition cost less collateral value (net of haircut) less any HJ; CMT (CMLF/CMF) — commodities pre-sale measured at acquisition cost less commodity collateral value (no market charge if binding promise and enforceable documentation), receivable at counterparty RW; Salam — supplier RW (100% unrated) until delivery, market risk 15% net + 3% gross with parallel Salam (no netting of credit exposures between Salam and parallel Salam), 15% on long position without parallel Salam (paras 299-312, 318-322, 330-338)

Contract stage capital (Istisnā`, Ijārah): Istisnā` receivables at ultimate buyer RW (100% unrated); 'exposure to asset' project finance slotted at 70/90/115/250%; advance-payment portions 0% RW; WIP: 1.6% (20% RW) market charge on unbilled WIP with credit RW (seller, no parallel), 15% (187.5% RW) as buyer without parallel Istisnā`; Ijārah/IMB — binding PL exposure = acquisition cost less asset collateral less HJ; lease receivables risk-weighted by lessee rating net of leased-asset collateral value; operating Ijārah residual value 100% RW and 15% charge on carrying value after lease expiry; IMB residual value risk borne by lessee (paras 354-362, 377, 390-399)

Sukūk and securitisation: rated Sukūk use ECAI ratings; unrated follow underlying contract treatment (e.g. Salam Sukūk supplier RW plus commodity market risk; Istisnā` Sukūk 100% + 20% price-risk add-on or slotting 70-250%; Mushārakah/Muḍārabah Sukūk as equity exposures); asset-based Sukūk without legal transfer carry the originator's RW; asset derecognition requires true sale, no effective control, claims only on the asset pool, SPE transferee and clean-up calls ≤10%; credit enhancement/retained securitisation exposures risk-weighted 20/50/100/350/1250% (AAA to B+ and below/unrated); deduction = 1250% RW; liquidity facilities 50% CCF (100% if externally rated); Qarḍ-based servicer cash advances 0% at discretion (paras 480, 492, 498-525, 529-530, 535-536)

Real estate: financing exposures follow the underlying contract sections with preferential RWs where eligible; direct real estate investment (including non-binding-stage holdings beyond a supervisory holding period such as six months) 187.5% RW (15% charge); operating Ijārah treated as investment; investment in a real estate subsidiary above 15% of regulatory capital risk-weighted 1250% (portion below 15% not lower than 100%); joint ventures 400% (unlisted)/300% (listed) or slotting per Appendix E; valuations at least annually for collateral (paras 545, 552-554(d), 559-562)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: eligible third-party guarantees are described as given for a fixed period and limited amount 'without any consideration being received by the guarantor'; a Muḍārib or Wakīl may not guarantee capital or returns, but a third party may guarantee Muḍārabah or Wakālah capital on the basis of Tabarru' (donation), in which case the guarantor's RW substitutes if lower

IFSB: CMT is recognised and given full capital treatment as interbank liquidity placement (CMLF) and customer financing (CMF), incorporating GN-2; but reverse CMT deposits (also called 'tawwaruq deposits') 'are a form of leverage, which, together with CMT-based term financing, has the potential to create unlimited debt in the system', and CMT-based term deposits are not loss-absorbent, increasing procyclicality

IFSB: 'It is not considered permissible in most jurisdictions to securitise debt claims or other receivables for the purpose of issuing tradable Sukūk', except where debts are incidental to physical assets/usufruct or a whole-entity sale; Salam Sukūk are 'generally considered to be non-tradable' as receivables; Murābahah Sukūk 'are not generally considered tradable in most jurisdictions'; mixed pools are tradable only if non-financial assets are not less than a certain minimum ratio

IFSB: 'Gold, silver and currency fall under foreign exchange risk in accordance with the Sharī`ah rules and principles that require the exchange of currencies to be made in an equal amount and on a spot basis' (unlike Basel, which treats silver as commodity risk); 'A binding bilateral promise in an exchange of currencies is equivalent to a forward contract, which is prohibited by Sharī`ah jurists in most (but not all) countries'; net positions of unilateral binding promises to buy/sell currencies or gold/silver are included in the FX open position

IFSB: the distinction between binding and non-binding MPO 'are subject to the criteria and opinions set out by the respective Sharī`ah Supervisory Board (SSB) of the IIFS or any other SSB as specified by the supervisory authority'; an agreement to lease 'may be considered as binding (binding PL) or as non-binding (non-binding PL), depending on the applicable Sharī`ah interpretations'; Hamish Jiddiyah is eligible CRM only where the promise is binding; a Muḍārib, Sharik or Wakīl may not undertake in advance to repurchase Sukūk assets at nominal/par value, though repurchase at net asset, market or fair value or an agreed price at time of purchase is permissible, and a lessee-originator may undertake to purchase leased assets at nominal value

divergence_notes: Sharī`ah requirements for financing contracts: 'The list is not conclusive and may vary according to the views of different Sharī`ah boards' (para 263)

Binding bilateral currency promise 'is equivalent to a forward contract, which is prohibited by Sharī`ah jurists in most (but not all) countries as the delivery of one or both countervalues is deferred' (fn 75)
True sale criteria apply 'From a juristic perspective, subject to jurists' interpretations in the jurisdiction' (para 461)

In jurisdictions with legal impediments to transferring legal ownership (e.g. sovereign assets), only beneficial ownership is transferred, producing asset-based rather than asset-backed Sukūk, with recourse to the originator; IDB Sharī`ah Board conditions for such transfers are set out (paras 449, 452; fn 115)
Securitising debt claims for tradable Sukūk 'is not considered permissible in most jurisdictions', with exceptions for incidental debts (fn 113)
References to Sharī`ah rules 'do not encompass all the practices followed by IIFS in different jurisdictions' and the IFSB expresses no opinion on Sharī`ah compliance of products (para 18)
Some Wakālah-based accounts are 'constructed such that it has an element of fixed return and/or capital guarantee, which makes it closer to a deposit account than a PSIA' (fn 84)
Payments in advance under Salam permitted 'upon execution of a Salam contract or within a subsequent period not exceeding two or three days as deemed permissible by its SSB' (para 325)
Penalty clauses for delay: not permitted in Salam, 'however, it is allowed under Istisnā` or parallel Istisnā`' (para 263(b)(ii))
Classification of MPO promises as binding or non-binding, and treatment of Musāwamah and Bay` Bithaman Ajil, are left to SSB opinions and supervisory discretion (paras 291-292)

standards.applicability: Guidance for supervisory authorities supervising IIFS in the banking segment, excluding Islamic insurance (Takāful) institutions and Islamic collective investment schemes (para 6). Primarily intended to guide firm-level supervision of full-fledged banking IIFS — including commercial banks, investment banks and other fund-mobilising institutions — with due consideration to 'proportionality' taking account of size, sophistication and complexity (para 20). Supervisory authorities may, at their discretion, extend application to self-contained Islamic 'window' operations or other IIFS in their jurisdictions (para 21); windows are dealt with specifically in section 3.8 (paras 184-198). Macroprudential responsibilities are acknowledged but not treated in detail (para 25). Scope and application determined by reference to adoption of the other applicable IFSB Standards (para 20).
standards.structure: Not principles-numbered; organised in four sections plus Definitions. SECTION I: INTRODUCTION — 1.1 Background (paras 1-5); 1.2 Main Premises and Objectives (paras 6-10); 1.3 General Principles (paras 11-19); 1.4 Scope and Application (paras 20-25); 1.5 Stock-taking Initiative (para 26); 1.6 Implementation Date (para 27). SECTION II: SUPERVISORY PRECONDITIONS, CRITERIA AND APPROACHES FOR EFFECTIVE SUPERVISION OF IIFS — 2.1 Necessary Preconditions (paras 28-33); 2.2 Criteria for Classifying the Institution as an IIFS or Window (paras 34-35); 2.3 Additional Considerations in the Issuance of an IIFS Licence (paras 36-37); 2.4 Supervisory Approaches (paras 38-41). SECTION III: KEY ELEMENTS IN THE SUPERVISORY REVIEW PROCESS OF IIFS — 3.1 Regulatory Capital Requirements (paras 42-64: components/buffers, slotting method, additional operational risk charges, IAH/DCR/smoothing/alpha, advanced approaches); 3.2 Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (paras 65-83, incl. four Basel II Pillar 2 principles at para 66); 3.3 Governance and Risk Management (paras 84-135: corporate governance, Sharī`ah governance, risk management process, enterprise-wide risk management); 3.4 Related Party Transactions (paras 136-141); 3.5 Securitisation Risk and Related Off-balance Sheet Exposures (paras 142-154); 3.6 Transparency and Market Discipline (paras 155-162); 3.7 Consolidated and Home-host Supervision (paras 163-183, incl. supervisory colleges and cross-border insolvency); 3.8 Islamic Window Operations (paras 184-198). SECTION IV: ADDITIONAL SPECIFIC ISSUES — 4.1 Risk Concentration incl. real estate limits (paras 200-217); 4.2 Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book (paras 218-225); 4.3 Counterparty Credit Risk (paras 226-229); 4.4 Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision (paras 230-235); 4.5 Sound Stress Testing Practices (paras 236-245); 4.6 Reputational Risk (paras 246-250); 4.7 Sharī`ah-compliant Hedging Techniques (paras 251-253); 4.8 Valuation Practices (paras 254-256); 4.9 Supervisory Transparency and Accountability (paras 257-259). DEFINITIONS (Alpha, Commodity Murābahah, DCR, Governance Committee, Hamish al-Jiddiyyah, IRR, Muḍārabah, Mushārakah, PER, SSB, Sukūk, Sukūk securitisation, Takāful, Urbūn).
key_points: Revises and replaces IFSB-5 (December 2007) on the supervisory review process, updating for post-2008 crisis reforms including Basel 2.5, Basel III and the BCBS July 2009 Pillar 2 enhancements; Council approved the revision at its 19th meeting on 17 November 2011 (paras 1-6)
A stock-taking survey ran from 24 October to 30 November 2012 across all 38 IFSB banking regulatory and supervisory authorities, receiving 35 responses (92% response rate) (para 26, fn 8)
Implementation date: members expected to apply the Standard from January 2015, transposed into national supervisory guidelines and reflected in supervisory manuals/handbooks (para 27)

Supervisory authority may require an IIFS to use either the Standard Formula or the Supervisory Discretion Formula of IFSB-15; under the Standard Formula IAH are treated as investors rather than depositors, shifting supervisory emphasis to investor protection rather than capital requirements on IAH-funded assets (paras 16-17)

Preconditions for effective supervision adapted from revised Basel Core Principles; as IIFS cannot use conventional interest-based LOLR facilities, Sharī`ah-compliant LOLR contingency arrangements are necessary and supervisors should clarify their roles as providers of Sharī`ah-compliant liquidity support (paras 28-32)

Eligible capital requirements must be not less than 8% of total risk-weighted assets at all times, with CET1 of at least 4.5% of RWA, Tier 1 (CET1 plus AT1) of at least 6.0% of RWA, and total capital (Tier 1 plus Tier 2) of at least 8.0% of RWA; D-SIBs must hold additional CET1, and R-SIBs or globally systemic IIFS may be considered (paras 47)

CET1 and AT1 are 'going concern' capital absorbing losses while solvent; Tier 2 is 'gone concern' capital protecting current account holders and creditors on non-viability; capital conservation buffer, countercyclical capital buffer and leverage ratio to be operationalised across the industry in line with IFSB-15 (paras 48-49)

For Mushārakah or Muḍārabah financing contracts, supervisors should provide specific guidance on the supervisory slotting method as an alternative to the simple risk-weight method, referring to criteria in Appendices E and F of IFSB-15; any lower RW requires robust supervisory review of factors such as collateral quality, financial controls and exit strategies (paras 50-52)

Supervisors have discretion to impose additional operational-risk capital charges for Sharī`ah non-compliance risk, based on factors including precedents of material non-compliance, robustness of ex-ante/ex-post Sharī`ah governance, internal Sharī`ah audit, and availability of a Sharī`ah review function; strong mitigating governance may nullify the need for the add-on (paras 53-55)

Treatment of unrestricted IAH for CAR varies by jurisdiction — from full exclusion of IAH-funded assets to treatment as liabilities (the latter 'in the opinion of the Sharī`ah Board of the IDB is not Sharī`ah compliant'); under the supervisory discretion formula a proportion alpha of risk-weighted assets funded by unrestricted PSIA is included in the CAR denominator, alpha near 0 reflecting IAH as investors and alpha close to 1 reflecting IAH as depositors (paras 56, 61, fn 28)

GN-4 provides the methodology for measuring DCR and estimating alpha; smoothing techniques include forfeiting the Muḍārib share of profits, donation of profits by shareholders, maintenance of PER to smooth returns, and IRR solely to cover IAH losses — supervisors approving smoothing must issue a written policy on assessing DCR exposure (paras 57-60)

IFSB-15 covers only the standardised approach; supervisors may at their discretion allow migration to advanced approaches (foundation/advanced IRB, AMA) subject to robustness of internal models, sufficient reliable data and other requirements, with validation capacity including quantitative modelling expertise (paras 44, 62-64)

ICAAP rests on the four Basel II Pillar 2 principles and five features: board and senior management oversight, comprehensive assessment of risks, sound capital assessment, monitoring and reporting, and internal control review; risks not (fully) covered by Pillar 1 include DCR, liquidity risk, credit concentration risk, rate of return risk in the banking book, SNCR, legal and reputational risk (paras 66-78)

Supervisors should require an ICAAP document submission, may set trigger and target capital ratios or categories above minima (e.g. well capitalised/adequately capitalised), and should intervene early — remedial options include intensified monitoring, restricting dividends, capital restoration plans and immediate capital raising (paras 80-83)

Corporate governance review covers SSB qualification criteria, a Governance Committee (per IFSB-3) specifically mandated to protect IAH interests when the IIFS acts as Muḍārib or Wakīl, control-function compensation independence, mechanisms for reporting Sharī`ah non-compliance (SSB direct reporting, disclosure, inspections, whistle-blowing, customer complaints), and regular annual combined discussions with BOD, Audit Committee and SSB (paras 87-96)

Sharī`ah governance system must cover ex-ante processes (issuance of pronouncements, pre-offering compliance checks) and ex-post processes (internal Sharī`ah review and reporting), with annual Sharī`ah compliance review/audit; supervisors should at minimum enforce IFSB-10 (paras 97-101)

ERM framework must incorporate IIFS-specific risks — equity investment risk in the banking book, rate of return risk, DCR, SNCR and fiduciary risk — and track 'transformation of risk' at contractual stages (e.g. in Murābahah, market risk transforms into credit risk after sale on deferred terms); SNCR has two aspects: failure of the Sharī`ah governance mechanism, and SSB rulings coming under criticism (paras 117-120)

Securitisation review: implicit (non-contractual) support raises Sharī`ah concerns — it is not permissible for the Muḍarib, Shārik or Wakīl to undertake in advance to repurchase assets from Sukūk holders at nominal or par value, except at net asset value at time of purchase; SPEs must be bankruptcy-remote via 'true sale' (four juristic criteria, IFSB-15 section 5.2.4), and if remoteness is in doubt the SPE should be consolidated for capital adequacy (paras 142-154, fn 57, fn 59)

Islamic windows: defined as part of a conventional institution (branch or dedicated unit, not a separate legal entity) providing both Sharī`ah-compliant fund management and financing; 'asset-side only windows' are distinguished; window capital may be computed via the CAR denominator then deducted from parent CET1; supervisors may require conversion into full-fledged IIFS/subsidiaries by size criteria; the survey found 160 Islamic windows (50 in one jurisdiction, 24 in another), mostly operating over 15 years, and in some cases Islamic window financing assets exceed one-third of the parent's balance sheet (paras 184-198, fn 72, fn 79)

Concentration risk: large exposure limits for single counterparties mostly range 10-35% of the IIFS's capital base across jurisdictions; supervisory actions for breaches include warnings, ICAAP capital add-ons and deduction of the excess from the capital base; CMT and real estate concentrations are common in IIFS portfolios (paras 200-206, fn 80)

Real estate investment limits: aggregate limit relative to regulatory capital with significantly lower single-exposure limit, or alternatively separate limits for own funds/current accounts versus UIAH funds (e.g. 15% of UIAH funds); no proposed limit on restricted investment accounts dedicated to real estate; punitive capital requirements (deduction from capital) possible for over-concentration (paras 212-213)

Rate of return risk in the banking book is dealt with under Pillar 2, not a mandatory Pillar 1 charge; supervisors should be particularly attentive to 'outlier IIFS' whose ROR risk leads to an economic value decline of more than 20% of the sum of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital following a standardised benchmark rate shock; BCBS recommends a 200 basis point parallel shock but authorities may adjust for local context (paras 220, 225, fn 88)

Counterparty credit risk is relevant to CMT practices (OTC or organised markets): CMLF for interbank/central bank liquidity operations, CMF for financing where the counterparty sells commodities spot; IIFS should manage CCR through credit policies, Takāful coverage, collateral and authorised limits before entering CMT (paras 226-229, fn 89, fn 90)

Liquidity and stress testing supervision: Basel III LCR ensures survival of an acute stress scenario lasting a month, complemented by the NSFR; an SLRP is required in conjunction with an IIFS ILAAP; stress testing compliance is assessed against Principles 3.1 to 3.22 of IFSB-13 with GC and SSB involvement; valuation review covers daily mark-to-market and mark-to-model practices for infrequently traded Sukūk (paras 235, 239-240, 254-256)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: CMT ('Commodity Murābahah transactions as a tool for liquidity management') is a Murābahah-based purchase and sale transaction of Sharī`ah-compliant commodities, on cash or deferred payment terms (Definitions); it is treated as an accepted but prudentially sensitive practice — GN-2 notes high concentrations in IIFS portfolios (para 201), CMT-based deposits create SNCR exposure on the liabilities side (para 119), and CMT (CMLF/CMF) may involve significant counterparty credit risk requiring credit policies, Takāful coverage, collateral and authorised limits before entering CMT (paras 227-229)

IFSB: the use of Sharī`ah-compliant hedging instruments (Sharī`ah-compliant alternatives to derivatives contracts) 'is still not a common practice among IIFS, owing to strict Sharī`ah prohibitions; however, there is evidence that IIFS are employing certain OTC hedging instruments on the basis that they are Sharī`ah compliant' — including profit rate swaps and cross currency swaps used in some jurisdictions, with underlying contracts ranging from CMT to Wa`d and combinations of other contracts; supervisors should require aggregated risk analysis, IFSB-15 capital treatment, collateral posting and reporting (paras 251-253)

IFSB: implicit support to securitisations raises Sharī`ah concerns — 'According to Sharī`ah rules and principles as generally understood, it is not permissible for the Muḍarib (investment manager), Shārik (partner) or Wakīl (agent) to undertake in advance to repurchase assets from Sukūk holders or from one who holds them, for their nominal or par value, except on the basis of the net asset value, at the time of purchase' (fn 57); repurchase undertakings by IIFS at values other than market value of Sukūk assets are flagged as a reputational risk source (para 247); Hamish al-Jiddiyyah carries limited recourse when a purchase orderer fails to honour a binding promise to purchase (PP) or promise to lease (PL) (Definitions); Wa`d appears among underlying contracts for Sharī`ah-compliant hedging instruments (fn 98)

divergence_notes: Treatment of UIAH for CAR 'varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction'; in some jurisdictions IAH are treated like a liability of the IIFS 'which therefore bears the risk of the assets funded by IAH "(which in the opinion of the Sharī`ah Board of the IDB is not Sharī`ah compliant)"' (para 56, fn 28)

Second aspect of SNCR: 'the risk that the rulings given by the IIFS's SSB or other body come under criticism and are not generally accepted, again leading to the loss of current or future business' (para 120)

Aggregation across groups 'is particularly significant in Islamic finance because of the possibility that aggregation will be based on interpretations of, for example, the status of IAH which may be different from those prevailing in the jurisdiction in question' (fn 52)
'From a juristic perspective, subject to jurists' interpretations in the jurisdiction, there are four key criteria for a transaction to be considered as a "true sale"' (fn 59)
In home-host relationships, supervisors must consider 'national Sharī`ah interpretations' among competing pressures (para 164)

At the consolidated level, 'in particular, in cases where the Sharī`ah is being interpreted differently across countries', supervisors should promote harmonisation of legal and Sharī`ah compliance frameworks, collaboration between SSBs of various jurisdictions, and sharing of rulings and their bases (para 168)

'There are diverse approaches with respect to regulation and supervision of Sharī`ah matters in various jurisdictions' — some have a national Sharī`ah board, others only require applicable Sharī`ah systems (para 170)
Supervisory college scope should include 'divergence of Sharī`ah compliance practices and integration of SSBs' (para 179)

Court cases in the IFSI include 'conflict of jurisdiction of a civil law or common law court vis-à-vis the Sharī`ah court' and 'applicability of civil law principles to decide on disputes in Islamic financial transactions' (fn 50)

standards.applicability: Applies to the regulation and supervision of Islamic banking only; Takaful and Islamic capital markets are excluded and will get their own Core Principles later (para 6). Primarily guides firm-level supervision of full-fledged (separately incorporated) banking IIFS with due consideration to proportionality (size, sophistication, complexity), including commercial banks, investment banks and other fund-mobilising institutions (para 18). Islamic 'windows' (not separately incorporated) are addressed by a dedicated principle, CPIFR 32, with the other CPIFR also applying to windows subject to branch status and materiality (para 19). Non-bank financial institutions providing bank-like funds mobilisation may also be covered as appropriate (fn 3). Supervisory authorities should apply the CPIFR to all Islamic banking institutions within their jurisdictions (para 14); the CPIFR are intended for both dual banking environments and fully Islamic banking environments (para 62).

standards.structure: Section 1: Introduction (background, premises/objectives, general approach, scope, implementation date, structure, the 33 CPIFR in summary) (paras 1-25). Section 2: Preconditions for Effective Supervision of IIFS (macro policies, financial stability framework, public infrastructure, crisis management/recovery/resolution, systemic protection/safety net incl. SCDIS and SLOLR, market discipline) (paras 26-44). Section 3: Assessment Methodology for CPIFR (use, four-grade compliance assessment, practical considerations) (paras 45-62). Section 4: Criteria for Assessing Compliance (essential/additional criteria per principle) (paras 63-64). Appendix A: Mapping the BCPs to the CPIFR. Definitions. The 33 Core Principles (verbatim headings, Section 4): CPIFR 1: Responsibilities, objectives and powers (BCP 1); CPIFR 2: Independence, accountability, resourcing and legal protection for supervisors (BCP 2); CPIFR 3: Cooperation and collaboration (BCP 3); CPIFR 4: Permissible activities; CPIFR 5: Licensing criteria (BCP 5); CPIFR 6: Transfer of significant ownership (BCP 6); CPIFR 7: Major acquisitions; CPIFR 8: Supervisory approach (BCP 8); CPIFR 9: Supervisory techniques and tools; CPIFR 10: Supervisory reporting; CPIFR 11: Corrective and sanctioning powers of supervisors; CPIFR 12: Consolidated supervision; CPIFR 13: Home-host relationships; CPIFR 14: Treatment of investment account holders (IAHs); CPIFR 15: Corporate governance; CPIFR 16: Shari`ah governance framework; CPIFR 17: Risk management process; CPIFR 18: Capital adequacy; CPIFR 19: Credit risk; CPIFR 20: Problem assets, provisions and reserves; CPIFR 21: Concentration risk and large exposure limits; CPIFR 22: Transactions with related parties; CPIFR 23: Country and transfer risks (BCP 21); CPIFR 24: Equity investment risk; CPIFR 25: Market risk ('Market risks' in Section 1.7 listing); CPIFR 26: Rate of return risk; CPIFR 27: Liquidity risk; CPIFR 28: Operational risk; CPIFR 29: Internal control and audit; CPIFR 30: Financial reporting and external audit (BCP 27); CPIFR 31: Transparency and market discipline; CPIFR 32: Islamic 'windows' operations; CPIFR 33: Abuse of financial services (BCP 29). CPIFR 1-13 group: supervisory powers, responsibilities and functions; CPIFR 14-33 group: prudential regulations and requirements for IIFS.
key_points: The document sets out 33 Core Principles for Islamic Finance Regulation (CPIFR) for the banking segment, taking the BCBS Basel Core Principles and assessment methodology as revised in September 2012 as the starting point, with new principles added, some BCPs amended (mostly at criteria level) and others retained unchanged (paras 10-11).

Preparation of the CPIFR was approved by the IFSB Council at its 21st meeting on 12 December 2012 in Jeddah; the CPIFR deal only with Islamic banking — Takaful and Islamic capital markets are to get their own Core Principles in the future (paras 5-6).

Objectives include: a minimum international standard for supervision of IIFS; protecting consumers by ensuring any explicit or implicit claim to Shari`ah compliance is soundly based; safeguarding the linkage between the financial sector and the real economic sector; and ensuring IIFS act on their fiduciary responsibilities, especially to investors in PSIAs (para 8).

Implementation: the IFSB expects members to start implementing the standard from January 2016 (or later where an underlying IFSB standard applies later), transposed into national supervisory guidelines and manuals (para 23).

Each principle has essential criteria (the only basis for grading full compliance) and additional criteria (voluntary best practice aimed at jurisdictions with D-SIBs/R-SIBs); external assessments use a four-grade scale — compliant, largely compliant, materially non-compliant, non-compliant — plus 'not applicable', an issue especially relevant given the nascent state of Islamic finance in many jurisdictions (paras 12, 50-52).

Scope: firm-level supervision of full-fledged banking IIFS with proportionality; Islamic windows are covered by CPIFR 32 with the other CPIFR applying subject to branch status and materiality, an important aim being to avoid regulatory arbitrage within the jurisdiction (paras 18-19).

BCP mapping: many BCPs incorporated unchanged, several amended; BCP 23 (interest rate risk in the banking book) is replaced by CPIFR 26 (rate of return risk); five wholly new principles address IAH/PSIA treatment (CPIFR 14), Shari`ah governance (CPIFR 16), equity investment risk (CPIFR 24), rate of return risk (CPIFR 26) and Islamic windows (CPIFR 32) (para 64; Appendix A).

UIAH may be treated prudentially in one of three ways: (a) as investors bearing all earnings volatility and losses — the risk-weighted assets they finance are excluded from the capital adequacy denominator; (b) as a liability of the IIFS — an approach the Shari`ah board of the Islamic Development Bank considers not Shari`ah-compliant; or (c) as partially risk-absorbent — an 'alpha' proportion of the credit and market risk-weighted assets they finance is included in the denominator (CPIFR 14, Essential Criterion 1; fn 48).

Alpha (α) measures the proportion of actual credit and market risk on IAH-financed assets transferred to shareholders (the DCR); its value varies from 0 to 1, is dependent on the supervisory authority's directive, and GN-4 provides the estimation methodology (Definitions: Alpha).

Smoothing of profit payouts to IAH (to mitigate withdrawal risk) must be clearly indicated by IIFS; supervisors that approve smoothing techniques must issue a policy including criteria for assessing DCR exposure in capital adequacy; PER is appropriated out of Mudarabah profits before allocating the Mudarib's share, IRR out of IAH profits after the Mudarib's share (CPIFR 14, Essential Criteria 4 and 7; Definitions: PER, IRR).

Where real estate investment is permissible, supervisors must set prudential limits on the percentage of UIAH funds that may be invested in real estate and a single-exposure limit (CPIFR 14, Essential Criterion 8).

Shari`ah governance: a financial institution may not represent itself as 'Islamic' without the required governance structure; the Shari`ah board must be strong and independent (no member with blood or intimate relationship with the IIFS); the system must cover ex-ante processes (issuance of pronouncements, pre-offering compliance checks) and ex-post processes (internal and external Shari`ah review and reporting), with the Shari`ah board having free access to the ISCU and ISRU and an annual Shari`ah compliance review/audit (CPIFR 16, Essential Criteria 2, 3, 10-12; fn 60).

Corporate governance for IIFS must include Shari`ah compliance, the role of the Shari`ah board, IAH rights and investment-account transparency; a Governance Committee of at least three members — an Audit Committee member, a Shari`ah scholar and a non-executive director — is mandated to protect IAH interests; the supervisor holds regular combined meetings with BOD, Audit Committee and Shari`ah board (CPIFR 15, Essential Criteria 2, 9; fn 54).

Risk management must capture risks specific to IIFS — equity investment risk in the banking book, ROR risk, DCR, Shari`ah non-compliance risk and fiduciary risk — and 'transformation of risk' across contract stages (e.g. in Murabahah, market risk transforms into credit risk after sale on deferred terms) (CPIFR 17, Essential Criterion 8; fn 72).

Larger and more complex IIFS must have a dedicated risk management unit overseen by a CRO whose expertise includes the specificities of Islamic finance; CRO removal requires prior BOD approval, public disclosure and discussion with the supervisor (CPIFR 17, Essential Criterion 11).

Capital adequacy: regulatory capital components must comply with Shari`ah rules and principles; supervisors require the capital conservation buffer, counter-cyclical buffer and leverage ratio (per IFSB-15) adapted to IIFS balance sheets, capital treatment of Sukuk issuance/securitisation roles (originator, servicer, credit enhancer), and a capital adequacy approach reflecting risk-sharing with IAH and the resultant DCR/alpha (CPIFR 18, Essential Criteria 2 and 4).

Credit risk: IIFS must recognise potential credit exposures arising at different stages of financing agreements, carry out due diligence before choosing the Islamic financing instrument, manage counterparty performance risk in Salam and Istisna` contracts, and use Shari`ah-compliant risk mitigating techniques (permissible, enforceable collateral and guarantees) (CPIFR 19, Essential Criterion 4).

Problem assets: homogeneous portfolios are classified when payments are contractually in arrears for a minimum number of days (e.g. 30, 60, 90 days); the prohibition of Riba does not allow refinancing debts at renegotiated higher markup rates, though rescheduling without increasing the debt is allowed; supervisors must establish criteria for dealing with non-wilful defaulters where recognised (CPIFR 20, Essential Criteria 5 and 13; fn 87).

Large exposures: 10% or more of an IIFS's capital is defined as a large exposure and 25% of capital is the limit for an individual large exposure to a private-sector non-bank counterparty or group of connected counterparties; concentration risk arising from UPSIAs must be managed separately as well as in aggregate (CPIFR 21, Essential Criteria 4 and 9).

ROR risk in the banking book is the Islamic analogue of interest rate risk; it leads to DCR if the IIFS absorbs shortfalls in IAH returns by reducing its Mudarib share or by donation from shareholders' income; IIFS must maintain an informed judgment on appropriate PER balances whose essential function is DCR mitigation, and supervisors assess IAHs' behavioural and maturity profiles (fn 107; CPIFR 26, Essential Criteria 3 and 8).

Liquidity: IIFS must hold adequate liquidity for cash withdrawal requirements of current account holders, UIAH, (in some cases) RIAH, and commodity Murabahah transaction (CMT)-based deposits (reverse Murabahah); LCR and NSFR application guidance is in GN-6; conventional LOLR/discount windows involve interest so are unusable by IIFS, hence Shari`ah-compliant LOLR contingency arrangements and a clear supervisory policy statement on Shari`ah-compliant liquidity support are required, and an SCDIS applying to UPSIA is a key systemic-protection element (CPIFR 27, Essential Criteria 4 and 10; fn 110; paras 40-41).

Operational risk explicitly includes legal, fiduciary and Shari`ah non-compliance risk (excluding strategic and reputational risk); IIFS must keep track of income recognised from Shari`ah non-compliant sources, assess profits that cannot be recognised as eligible, and consider Shari`ah non-compliance risk as part of operational risk under ICAAP (fn 112; CPIFR 28, Essential Criteria 8-9).

Islamic windows: supervisors define permitted forms ('full windows' vs 'asset-side only windows'); windows need a minimum amount of funding from the conventional parent, transparent segregation of Islamic assets and funds (preventing investment in non-compliant assets and channelling investors' funds back to the parent), Shari`ah governance comparable to full-fledged IIFS, a full separate set of financial statements, and clearly specified criteria where a policy requires conversion into Islamic banking subsidiaries (CPIFR 32, Essential Criteria 1-3, 5, 9, 11; fn 119).

Abuse of financial services: IIFS need strict CDD rules with a group-wide programme including enhanced due diligence for high-risk accounts and politically exposed persons, and CDD/transaction records with at least a five-year retention period; staff reporting suspicious activity in good faith cannot be held liable (CPIFR 33, Essential Criteria 5 and 11).

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: IFSB-17 treats commodity Murabahah transactions (CMT) as an accepted Shari`ah-compliant tool — defining 'commodity Murabahah transactions as a tool for liquidity management' as 'a Murabahah-based purchase and sale transaction of Shari`ah-compliant commodities, whether on cash or deferred payment terms' — and requires IIFS to hold adequate liquidity for the potential cash withdrawal requirements of CMT-based deposits (reverse Murabahah); GN-2 (December 2010) is the referenced standard for CMT risk management and capital adequacy.
clauses: fn 111 (CMT-based assets and liabilities in liquidity stress scenarios)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: 'Gold, silver and currency fall under foreign exchange risk in accordance with the Shari`ah rules and principles that require the exchange of currencies to be made in an equal amount and on a spot basis. On the other hand, the Basel 1996 Market Risk Amendment (Section A3) treats gold as being under foreign exchange risk, and silver as being under commodity risk.' — i.e. IFSB classifies gold, silver and currency together under FX risk on Shari`ah grounds (spot, equal-amount exchange), diverging from the Basel treatment of silver.

IFSB: notes that 'the non-binding promise and legal enforcement aspects vary among IIFS or from one jurisdiction to another, which may give rise to operational risks and other risk management problems relating to Shari`ah compliance'; the Ijarah definition has the contract commence 'with a promise to lease that is binding on the part of the potential lessee'; in Diminishing Musharakah one partner 'promises to buy' the other's equity, the buying/selling must be independent of the partnership contract and not stipulated in it; Hamish al-Jiddiyyah carries limited recourse to the extent of damages when the purchase orderer 'fails to honour a binding promise to purchase (PP) or promise to lease (PL)'.

divergence_notes: On treating UIAH as a liability of the IIFS: 'In the opinion of the Shari`ah board of the Islamic Development Bank, this approach is not Shari`ah-compliant.' (fn 48, on CPIFR 14, Essential Criterion 1(b))

Consolidated supervision must address 'cases where the Shari`ah is being interpreted differently across jurisdictions'; supervisors are to promote harmonisation of legal and Shari`ah compliance frameworks, collaboration between Shari`ah boards in various jurisdictions, and sharing of rulings and their bases (CPIFR 12, Essential Criterion 3)
Cross-border Islamic financial services lead to 'increased complications when conducting CPIFR assessments, especially given differences in, for example, interpretations of Shari`ah' (para 61)

Shari`ah governance models vary: 'in some jurisdictions, there is a national body (e.g. a national Shari`ah Council) that has the authority to issue Fatawa... that are mandatory for IIFS in that jurisdiction, while in the majority of jurisdictions it is an IIFS's Shari`ah board that issues Fatawa' — IFSB-10 suggests no 'single model' or 'one-size-fits-all' approach (fn 59, on CPIFR 16)

Early repayment rebate practice differs: 'in certain jurisdictions, IIFS may accept full settlement but give rebates on subsequent transactions, while in other jurisdictions the IIFS may give rebates immediately at their discretion without any reference to this in the contract' (fn 109, on CPIFR 26); similarly, early-settlement discounts may be given as a discretionary commercial decision provided not stated in the contract (fn 89, on CPIFR 20)

'In jurisdictions where non-wilful defaults are recognised by practice, the supervisory authority establishes criteria and procedures for dealing with non-wilful defaulters.' (CPIFR 20, Essential Criterion 13)

Understanding the Concept of Retakāful and its Underlying Contracts: concept, principal structures in use, core principles, categorisation, windows, Retakāful business of TUs, types of Retakāful, special issues, regulatory standards and practices (paras 12-34). C. The Guiding Principles, in five parts: I Governance of Retakāful Undertakings — PRINCIPLE 1.1 'Comprehensive Governance Framework' (paras 35-43); PRINCIPLE 1.2 'Code of Ethics and Conduct' (paras 44-54); PRINCIPLE 1.3 'Truthfulness, Honesty and Fairness' (paras 55-65); PRINCIPLE 1.4 'Due Care and Diligence' (paras 66-70); PRINCIPLE 1.5 'Systems and Procedures' (paras 71-75); II Compliance with Sharī`ah Principles — PRINCIPLE 2.1 'Business is Sharī`ah-Compliant' (paras 76-87); III Prudential Framework — PRINCIPLE 3.1 'Adequate Risk Management Framework' (paras 88-94); PRINCIPLE 3.2 'Solvency of Retakāful Undertakings' (paras 95-108); PRINCIPLE 3.3 'Investment Strategy' (paras 109-114); IV Transparency and Disclosure — PRINCIPLE 4.1 'Appropriate Disclosures' (paras 115-118); V Supervisory Review of Retakāful/Reinsurance Arrangements — PRINCIPLE 5.1 'Supervision of Retakāful /reinsurance Programmes' (paras 119-127). D. Definitions. E. Appendix: generic flow of funds under Wakālah, Wakālah-Muḍārabah, Wakālah-Waqf, Saudi Cooperative and Sudan Cooperative models.
key_points: Retakāful is the Islamic alternative to conventional reinsurance comprising both Family and General business; participants are mainly TUs and occasionally other RTUs ('Retrotakāful'), who as cedants contribute from their PRFs or cedant RRFs as Tabarru' into a common fund managed by the receiving RTO (para 4)
Whereas conventional reinsurance typically involves contractual transfer of risk from cedant to reinsurer, Retakāful arrangements provide for sharing, rather than transfer, of risks (para 4)
Development of the standard was approved by the IFSB Council at its 23rd meeting, held in Doha, Qatar, on 11 December 2013 (para 2)
IFSB-10, IFSB-11 and IFSB-14 are applicable to Retakāful; IFSB-8 and IFSB-9 are only partially applicable, and the document does not intend to supersede these standards (para 7)
The standard draws on IAIS Insurance Core Principle 13 'Reinsurance and Other Forms of Risk Transfer', in the version as amended on 12 October 2012 (para 8, fn 5)
An IFSB survey conducted 10 July - 15 August 2014 received 67 respondents: 14 RTOs, 38 TOs and 15 RSAs (fn 17)

Four principal structures in use: Wakālah (pre-agreed Wakālah fee, usually a percentage of contributions, covering management expenses, distribution costs and a margin of operational profit; RTO does not share in RRF risk or investment profit); Wakālah-Muḍārabah (RTO as Wakil for underwriting and Mudarib for investment with a predetermined percentage share of investment profit); Wakālah-Waqf (shareholders and potentially cedants contribute seed money to a Waqf RRF, RTO acts as Waqif and Wakil); and Cooperative (para 17)

The Saudi and Sudan cooperative models differ: in the Saudi model the RTO receives a predetermined share of underwriting surplus from the Cooperative RRF; the Sudan model does not allow surplus sharing — all surplus belongs to the cedants and the RTO is remunerated via a predetermined share of investment income as Mudarib (fn 11)

Core principles of Takāful and Retakāful are Tabarru', Ta'awun and prohibition of Riba; use of Tabarru' renders the element of Gharar acceptable because the contract is not an exchange contract (Aqad al-mu'awdah) (para 19, fn 13)

The IIFA (Resolution 200 (6/21), 21st meeting, Riyadh, 18-20 November 2013) resolved that Islamic insurance companies should reinsure only with Islamic reinsurance companies except where not possible and 'for other valid reasons', and then only within parameters set by the Sharī`ah committee (para 21, fn 12)

A Family Retakāful arrangement will not normally include a PIF, since the PIF is a pure investment fund whose investment risks are fully borne by the Takāful participants; contributions flow from the TU's PRF to the RTU's RRF on the basis of Tabarru' (para 22)
An RTU permitted to undertake both Family and General Retakāful is likely to be required to maintain separate operational frameworks and separate RRFs for each (para 23)

Quota share example: under a 40% quota share contract the contribution payable to the RTU is based on 40% of the contribution received by the cedant (less a negotiated ceding commission) and 40% of claims incurred are recovered; surplus treaty example: retention of $20 million and limit of $100 million — risks under $20 million are not ceded, risks of $20-120 million are ceded in proportion (sum assured - $20 million)/sum assured, and above $120 million the proportion is $100 million/sum assured (para 27)

Excess-of-loss example: cover of $30 million excess of $20 million — the cedant bears the initial $20 million, recovers up to $30 million, and recovers no more than $30 million if the claim exceeds $50 million; stop-loss protects the whole account, with deductibles and limits typically expressed as loss ratios (para 27)

Financial or finite risk Retakāful arrangements — effectively borrower-lender relationships without pooling — are not generally regarded as Sharī`ah compliant due to the absence of pooling and potential lack of transparency; the IDB Sharī`ah Board does not consider them Sharī`ah-compliant (para 27, fn 21)

Sharī`ah non-compliance risk is heightened because it is ordinarily impracticable for RTUs to perform their own Sharī`ah assessment of every risk in bundled treaties; RTUs must place some reliance on cedants' Sharī`ah governance and need mechanisms for identifying and purifying tainted income (para 28)

Payment of profit commission based upon the result of a single cedant's risks is considered by some to conflict with the principle of risk sharing; crediting commission to a fund other than that which bore the contribution expense creates a conflict of interest (para 28)
In Europe, the Reinsurance Directive was passed in 2005 and European reinsurers are required to comply with the Solvency II regime (para 29)

Sharī`ah advisers of RTOs should ensure the presumption that underwriting surplus arising in the RRF is attributable to cedants and, if distributed, is distributed to the cedants' PRFs, with exceptions justified based on Sharī`ah; and that procedures exist for Sharī`ah assessment of Retrotakāful, profit commission, ceding commission, risks from conventional insurers, coinsurance with conventional reinsurers, supplementary activities, and purification of tainted income (para 85)

Where RRF assets are not fungible, the RTO must evaluate the capital adequacy of that RRF on a segregated basis, with no recognition of surplus assets in other RRFs and no diversification allowance; diversification may be taken into account only where assets are freely transferable between RRFs (para 103)

Qarḍ facility mechanics: assets earmarked in the SHF may count towards eligible capital of the RRF if local regulation permits; the RTO must consent to its RSA that the facility cannot be withdrawn before the RRF meets solvency requirements independently, and that in run-off or winding-up any drawn Qarḍ is treated as donated to the RRF to the extent necessary for cedant TUs' claims to be met; drawdowns should in principle be repaid from future RRF surpluses; no double-counting of Qarḍ assets for SHF solvency (paras 98, 106)

An RTO should carry out a forward-looking own risk and solvency assessment (ORSA), reviewed periodically and whenever circumstances change significantly, with results communicated to the governing body and the RSA (para 94)

Retakāful window operations must segregate and ring-fence window assets from the conventional host, robustly including under conditions of insolvency, and any capital or liquidity support from the conventional operation must be identified and Sharī`ah-compliant (paras 87, 101, 114)

Decisions justified by Dharurah (necessity) to use conventional reinsurance/retrocession should specify a term or trigger conditions for review, and review should take place at least annually; RSAs should consider whether heavy reliance on cessions to conventional reinsurers affects a licensee's suitability to hold a TU or RTU licence (paras 120, 125)
divergence_notes: 'Many scholars disagree with the RTO taking any percentage of an underwriting surplus under a Mudārabah contract, on the ground that an underwriting surplus is not a profit, though some consider that a performance fee may be permitted' (fn 10)
'The payment of profit commission based upon the result of a single cedant's risks is considered by some to conflict with the principle of risk sharing' (para 28; repeated at para 122)
'The Sharī`ah Board of the Islamic Development Bank does not consider financial, or finite risk, Retakāful arrangements as Sharī`ah-compliant' (fn 21)

Jurisdictional divergence between cooperative models: 'There is, however, a difference between the Saudi and Sudan cooperative models' — Saudi allows RTO a predetermined share of underwriting surplus; Sudan 'does not allow the sharing of surplus between the RTO and the cedants' (fn 11)
'there is also a risk, particularly in marginal cases, of different interpretations of the application of Sharī`ah between cedants and RTUs' (para 28)

The IIFA resolved that Islamic insurance companies 'should reinsure only with Islamic reinsurance companies except where that is not possible' and for other valid reasons, within parameters set by the Sharī`ah committee (para 21)
'The distinction between Family and General Takāful may vary between jurisdictions' (fn 15)

'From a Sharī`ah point of view, there is no obligation on an RTO to use capital in the SHF to cover a deficit in an RRF... However, RSAs will sometimes place such an obligation (Qard) on an RTO' (fn 6)
'The conditions considered by Sharī`ah advisers to justify a finding of Dharurah may change over time, creating a need for periodic review of decisions in this area' (para 120)

standards.applicability: Applicable only to ṣukūk and ICIS (para 3); aimed at ṣukūk representing proportional, undivided ownership right in tangible assets or a pool of tangible assets and other types of assets, and at ICIS investing in transferable securities (para 4). Addressed to RSAs as a basis to set disclosure rules, to assess disclosure frameworks specified by others, and to provide a framework for ICM participants and facilitate cross-border offerings (para 2). Disclosure requirements should be applied by RSAs to public offerings; RSAs may choose to apply some or all to private offerings (para 44). Not intended to affect exemptions RSAs give governments, governmental entities and multilateral financial institutions, though Sharīʻah boards may still require certain Sharīʻah disclosures (para 46). Applies to any instrument that is a ṣukūk or would appear to be a ṣukūk, irrespective of terminology used (para 52). ICIS provisions apply across all ICIS structures, open-ended and closed-ended (paras 126, 128); RSAs decide whether to extend to profit-sharing investment account structures (para 128). Not intended to apply to hedge funds (para 131). Does not address wider aspects of financial intermediation such as suitability or intermediary remuneration disclosures (para 5).

Section 2: The Guiding Principles — 2.1 General Principles: Principle G.1 'Clear and Accurate Information' (paras 16-24), Principle G.2 'Sufficient Information' (paras 25-33), Principle G.3 'Timely Information' (paras 34-41); 2.2 Ṣukūk Disclosure: Application (paras 42-50), Principle S.1 'General Disclosure Principles Applicable to Ṣukūk' (paras 51-59), Principle S.2 'Sharīʻah-related Disclosures for Ṣukūk' (paras 60-79), Principle S.3 'Structure-related Disclosures for Ṣukūk' (paras 80-118), Principle S.4 'Entities about which Disclosures Should be Made' (paras 119-125); 2.3 ICIS Disclosure: Application (paras 126-136), Principle C.1 'Sharīʻah-related Disclosures for ICIS' (paras 137-149), Principle C.2 'Operations-related Disclosures for ICIS' (paras 150-153), Principle C.3 'Specialist ICIS Disclosure' (paras 154-177: property funds, Islamic REITs, exchange traded funds, money market funds, private equity/venture capital funds, commodity funds). key_points: Standard originated from the 27th Technical Committee meeting of 11 June 2012, a September 2012 IFSB-IOSCO-Securities Commission Malaysia Roundtable (papers published September 2013), and the Council decision of 12 December 2012 in Jeddah to prepare a disclosure standard for ICM products (para 1)

Objectives: basis for RSAs to set disclosure rules for ṣukūk and ICIS, assess adequacy of disclosure frameworks specified by others, provide a comprehensive disclosure framework, and create greater harmonisation to facilitate cross-border offerings (para 2)

Covers initial disclosure (prospectus/offering document), periodic disclosure (e.g. annual or quarterly financial statements), immediate disclosure (price-sensitive developments), and point-of-sale disclosure via a key information document (KID) or fact sheet (para 5)

Standard supersedes IFSB-6, IFSB-9 and IFSB-10 only where it specifies disclosures in the same areas and by the same parties, to that extent only (para 7); it complements IOSCO standards but if in conflict, for ICM products only, this standard prevails (para 9)

Standard deals only with areas where ICM products require disclosures additional to or different from conventional counterparts, assuming RSAs implement it within a regime based on IOSCO standards (para 11)
RSAs are expected to start implementation in their jurisdictions by 1 July 2018 (para 14)

Principle G.1: information in offering documents must be clear, accurate and not misleading, particularly regarding Sharīʻah aspects; retail-targeted offerings should not assume familiarity with Islamic jurisprudence or Arabic terms, nor present key concepts in small print (paras 17-19)

Principle G.2: full disclosure of material information; if an instrument is held out as Sharīʻah-compliant, expressly or by implication (e.g. the word 'participation' in Turkey, or Arabic terms in non-Arabic text), Sharīʻah disclosure is necessary; risk disclosures should include Sharīʻah non-compliance risks (paras 27, 32, fn 6)

Principle G.3: timely disclosure of material information; investors in ṣukūk and ICIS are assumed sensitive to Sharīʻah issues, so timely disclosure is required of any matter reasonably likely to affect ongoing Sharīʻah compliance (paras 34, 39)

The standard applies to any instrument that is or would appear to be a ṣukūk irrespective of terminology; indicators include Arabic contract terms (aqd), references to Sharīʻah, or references to Sharīʻah scholars or boards (paras 52, 59)

Terminology: the SPV issuing entity is distinguished from the 'originator' (commercial party deploying proceeds) and the 'obligor' (actual source of periodic and final payments), which are often but not necessarily the same (para 50)

Ṣukūk intended as regulatory capital under Basel III or IFSB-15 must have specified loss-absorbency or convertibility characteristics depending on Additional Tier 1 or Tier 2 ranking, with detailed disclosure mandated by the banking supervisor (para 57, fn 12 citing IFSB-15 paras 27 and 29)

Principle S.2 requires disclosure of the Sharīʻah board or advisory firm, names, credentials and relationship of scholars to originator/obligor/arranger; national Sharīʻah governance arrangements; the review process and documents reviewed; and any fatwā with its rationale and applicable Sharīʻah principles, disclosed for each fatwā where more than one set of advisers approved (paras 64-69, fn 17)

Tradeability limitations set by the Sharīʻah board (e.g. trading only at par or at the outstanding amount owed on spot basis) must be disclosed with reasoning; if the ṣukūk may not be traded Sharīʻah-compliantly at negotiated prices, the offering document must bear a prominent legend (para 71)

Disclosure must state whether arrangements exist for purification payments on non-Sharīʻah-compliant income and for ta'wīḍ or other compensation on overdue amounts, including circumstances, party, rate, manner and utilisation; periodic disclosures must detail payments made (paras 72-73, 78); the IDBG Sharīʻah Board view is that such compensation is to be donated to charity (fn 20)

Disclosure must state the role (if any) of Sharīʻah in interpreting ṣukūk contracts; where courts are not bound to apply Sharīʻah, disclosure must state that national law would be applied and that the interpretation may not be consistent with Sharīʻah principles; arrangements for post-issuance Sharīʻah guidance (default, enforcement, amendment, restructuring) must be described (paras 76-77)

Principle S.3 requires structural and funds-flow diagrams of the ṣukūk structure, disclosure of the sequence of contracts where significant to Sharīʻah compliance, the name and translation of any nominate contract (aqd), and summaries of principal contracts including kafālah/guarantee or takāful/insurance risk transfers (paras 85-88)

Contract-specific disclosure lists are given for ijārah (asset, lease period, rental rate, sublease, termination, maintenance, takāful, re-transfer), istisnā` (asset, delivery date, consideration, subcontractors, security, warranties, rejection), mushārakah (partners, capital, manager, third-party kafālah, profit/loss allocation, tanāzul), murābaḥah (parties, assets, prices, ta'wīḍ, ibra', agent, security, wa'd, kafālah), muḍārabah (rabb al-māl and muḍārib, capital, venture, kafālah, rahn given by muḍārib, profit allocation, tanāzul), wakālah bil istithmār (wakīl identity, investments, kafālah, investment policy, fee including performance incentive fee), and salam (parties, commodity, capital, delivery date, security) (paras 90-96)

Underlying assets and ownership: disclosure must cover asset use, valuation basis and valuer, substitution arrangements, encumbrances, transfer mechanisms in and out of the structure (e.g. purchase/sale undertakings), precise legal interests without relying solely on terms like 'legal ownership', 'beneficial ownership' or 'usufruct right', and any limitations on ṣukūk holders' rights (paras 98-105)

The ultimate source of payments and recourse must be disclosed clearly and prominently, explaining any contractual limitations on disposing of or enforcing against underlying assets and that asset performance depends entirely on the obligor's performance; Sharīʻah-compliant credit enhancement (security, kafālah, guarantees) must be disclosed (paras 82, 108)

Disclosure must state whether the obligor has conventional debt and whether cross-default provisions link the ṣukūk and that debt in both directions; absence of either linkage must be disclosed with risks described; restructuring limits to Sharīʻah-compliant outcomes, insolvency treatment risks, SPV Sharīʻah constraints in insolvency, enforcement limits from ownership limitations, and legally untested provisions must all be disclosed (paras 109-115)

Principle S.4: disclosures normally required of an issuer (business description, financial statements) must also be made about the obligor where different; liability for defective disclosure should fall on obligor and originator as well as issuer; Sharīʻah advisors are experts and their consent to inclusion of names and fatwā must be stated (paras 119-125)

Principle C.1: an ICIS must disclose asset types and the compliance process, external screening lists/methodologies with scholars' names and fatwā, its own Sharīʻah board's names, qualifications, roles, review frequency and non-conformity controls, internal/external Sharīʻah audit processes, KID disclosures, annual Sharīʻah advisors' report, tainted income amounts and purification recipients, and zakāh arrangements, amounts, calculation basis and recipients (paras 139-149)

Principle C.2: prospectus must disclose how cash balances will be invested, use and forms of leverage, use of Sharīʻah-compliant hedging instruments, and any securities borrowing or lending, in each case with the reason or process for judging Sharīʻah compliance (para 152)

Principle C.3 specialist funds: Islamic property funds must disclose Sharīʻah-compliant redemption liquidity mechanisms, takāful or other insurance of properties, Sharīʻah-compliant mortgage processes, co-investor conventional financing, alternative title-holding mechanisms, and tenant-income benchmarks (paras 156-157); Islamic REITs inherit property fund disclosures with emphasis on tenants and tainted income (para 158); Islamic ETFs should be physical, not synthetic, and replicate an Islamic index (para 160); Islamic MMFs must disclose Sharīʻah-compliant instruments and the Sharīʻah ruling on any unit-value stabilisation mechanism, IOSCO Recommendations 12 and 13 applying, with ribā difficulties noted for stable-NAV funds (paras 164-167); Islamic private equity needs no additional specific disclosures but close supervision of Sharīʻah governance (para 173); salam-based commodity funds must disclose the commodities, confirmation that the capital of salam has been paid in advance, and how Sharīʻah conditions of salam will be implemented (paras 176-177)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: where a third party provides a kafālah or guarantee of capital in mushārakah, muḍārabah or wakālah ṣukūk (or any kafālah in murābaḥah ṣukūk), disclosure must identify the guarantor, any relationship to the ṣukūk obligor or issuer, the principal terms, amounts guaranteed and 'any expenses payable and confirming that the guarantee and the related expenses paid are Sharīʻah-compliant' — the standard treats permissibility of the guarantee and its related expenses as requiring case-by-case Sharīʻah confirmation and disclosure rather than as settled

IFSB: if the Sharīʻah board opining on the ṣukūk sees limitations on secondary-market tradeability (e.g. 'trading only at par or at the outstanding amount owed on spot basis'), these must be disclosed with reasoning, and a prominent legend is required if the ṣukūk may not be traded or transferred in a Sharīʻah-compliant manner at negotiated prices; the IDBG Shari'ah Board view is that ṣukūk based on the securitization of murābaḥah debts can only securitize these debts at nominal value and 'can only be traded in a Sharī‘ah-compliant manner at par or at the outstanding amount owed on spot basis'

IFSB: commodity derivatives (futures and options) 'raise Sharīʻah compliance issues'; any ICIS investing in commodities or commodity futures must meet Sharīʻah requirements covering 'the prohibition on short selling, or forward selling and the requirement for actual or constructive possession', though a commodity fund can be established on the basis of salam; gold bullion is cited as an asset type with transparent pricing and liquidity, and conventional funds may hold physical gold bullion directly

IFSB: any wa'd (undertaking) given to purchase the murābaḥah assets must be disclosed; purchase undertaking and sale undertaking mechanisms for transferring assets into and out of the ṣukūk structure, and any arrangement (such as a purchase undertaking) that transfers or mitigates ownership or price risks of underlying assets, must be disclosed; wa'd is defined as 'Undertaking to perform an act in the future related to someone else', and the ijārah definition notes the contract 'could be preceded by a unilateral binding promise from one of the contracting parties' — the standard mandates disclosure of wa'd arrangements without ruling on their bindingness

divergence_notes: Publicly accessible Sharīʻah disclosures 'may also help in the longer term to promote convergence of Sharīʻah interpretation in this market' — implying current divergence of interpretation among scholars in the ṣukūk market (para 61)

IFSB-10 'recognises that Sharīʻah governance may take several forms, and that jurisdictions have adopted diverse approaches to it'; the standard accommodates whatever Sharīʻah governance arrangements consistent with IFSB-10 apply (para 8)

For ICIS, 'some legal environments might leave the ICIS operator open to legal action founded solely on differing interpretations of Sharīʻah'; mitigations include a 'reasonable enquiry and reasonable belief' defence or submitting interpretation issues to a national-level Sharīʻah authority where one exists (para 136)

IDBG Sharī'ah Board minority-style view set out at length: ṣukūk assets must be undividedly owned by ṣukūk holders and registered in their names; where legal title transfer is prohibited, 'asset-based' ṣukūk may only be issued in a Sharī‘ah-compliant manner by observing stated beneficial-ownership conditions (fn 18, referenced again at fn 21 and fn 22)
IDBG Sharī'ah Board view on late-payment compensation in murābaḥah ṣukūk: 'such compensation is to be donated to charity' (fn 20)
IDBG Shari'ah Board view that murābaḥah-debt securitization ṣukūk may only be securitized at nominal value and traded at par or outstanding amount on spot basis (fn 14)

Where an issuance has been approved by more than one set of Sharīʻah Advisers, fatwā disclosures must be made for each fatwā issued — contemplating plural, potentially differing, Sharīʻah approvals of a single issuance (fn 17)

The precise legal interests in underlying assets must be disclosed 'without solely relying on terms such as "legal ownership", "beneficial ownership" or "usufruct right", whose meanings may vary across jurisdictions' (para 104)
