standards.structure: Section 1: Introduction - 1.1 Background, 1.2 Main Objectives, 1.3 Principles, 1.4 Scope and Application (paras 1-15). Section 2: Supervisory Approaches for Effective Supervision of Takāful/Retakāful - 2.1 Risk-based Approach (paras 20-28); 2.2 Supervisory Tools: 2.2.1 Supervisory Reporting (paras 30-33), 2.2.2 Off-site Monitoring (paras 34-38), 2.2.3 On-site Inspection (paras 39-46), 2.2.4 Supervisory Follow-up (paras 47-50), 2.2.5 Enforcement (paras 51-54), 2.2.6 Event-based Supervision (para 55), 2.2.7 Thematic Review (paras 56-58). Section 3: Key Elements in the Supervisory Review Process of Takāful/Retakāful Undertakings - 3.1 Corporate Governance (paras 59-68), 3.2 Sharīʻah Governance (paras 69-76), 3.3 Takāful Operational Framework (paras 77-84), 3.4 Capital Adequacy: 3.4.1 Available Capital (paras 85-93), 3.4.2 Eligibility of Capital (paras 94-101), 3.4.3 Determination of Capital Requirements (paras 102-108), 3.4.4 Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA) (paras 109-118), 3.5 Retakāful (paras 119-122), 3.6 Risk Management (paras 123-128), 3.7 Takāful and Retakāful Windows (paras 129-133). Section 4: Additional Specific Issues - 4.1 Group Supervision (paras 134-138), 4.2 Conduct of Business (paras 139-144), 4.3 Run-off (paras 145-150). Definitions section follows (not principle-numbered; the standard sets out principles by section rather than numbered principles).
key_points: The standard is based on recommendations of the paper 'Issues in Regulation and Supervision of Takāful (Islamic Insurance)' produced by the joint working group (JWG) established by the IFSB and IAIS in 2005; the JWG outlined four themes: corporate governance; financial and prudential regulation; transparency, reporting and market conduct; and supervisory review process (paras 1-2)

Four takāful-specific standards and one guidance note preceded it: IFSB-8 [December 2009], IFSB-11 [December 2010], GN-5 [March 2011], IFSB-14 [December 2013] and IFSB-18 [April 2016]; IFSB-9 and IFSB-10 apply generally to Islamic financial institutions (paras 3-4)

Objectives: minimum standards for an effective and efficient supervisory review process for TUs/RTUs; promote fair, safe and stable takāful and retakāful markets for the benefit and protection of participants; and promote international harmonisation of supervision and supervisor cooperation (para 8)

The standard sets principles, not quantitative prescriptions - it does not specify on-site inspection frequency, return formats or risk weightings; it must be applied with 'proportionality' to size, nature and complexity, with careful thought for microtakāful (November 2015 joint IFSB-IAIS microtakāful paper cited); for features common with conventional insurance users should have regard to the IAIS ICPs, in particular ICPs 9, 10, 11 and 12 (paras 10-12, fn 5)

Scope: TUs/RTUs under family, general or composite licences; extendable to windows; primarily entity-level supervision; written around the hybrid mutual/shareholder model but applicable with limited modifications to pure mutual models (e.g. Sudan) and the Saudi Arabian cooperative model (paras 13-15)

'Supervisory review process' means the criteria and tools of supervision: understanding undertakings' activities and risks, identifying threats to market functioning, and monitoring adherence to regulation; relevant risks for TUs/RTUs include Sharīʻah non-compliance, which RSAs must cover to the extent consistent with their (varying) responsibilities; the standard distinguishes regulation (setting rules) from supervision (paras 17-19)

A risk-based approach is advocated: supervisory plans combine potential impact and assessed probability of failure - low probability/low impact undertakings get baseline monitoring with infrequent on-site inspection, high/high undertakings attract close and continuous supervision, with continual review of the analysis (paras 21, 24)

Segregation of funds must be factored into impact/probability assessment - different PRFs carry different risk levels, one PRF may be affected by problems in another PRF or the SHF, and Sharīʻah non-compliance has both prudential and conduct-of-business impacts; earnings, capital and liquidity must support shocks affecting or arising from the SHF, PRF and PIF (paras 23, 27)

Captives: a pure captive represents the lowest regulatory risk (no unrelated participants); highest risk are captives underwriting risks for unrelated participants or compulsory third-party liability with direct recourse - these should be supervised like commercial TUs/RTUs; affinity-group captives are treated like any other takāful undertaking (para 28)

Supervisory reporting: a core of scheduled returns specified in regulation; fund segregation calls for reporting at fund level as well as TU/RTU level; RSAs supervising Shariah matters could obtain periodic Shariah board statements; TOs/RTOs must report promptly material changes (e.g. issue of additional capital, occurrence of large claims, emergence of a deficit at fund level) and submit annual audited financial statements; off-site monitoring should cover credit, market, underwriting, reserving, liquidity, operational, conduct of business, Sharīʻah non-compliance, legal, strategic and reputational risks (paras 30-35)

On-site inspection activities include valuation of assets, technical provisions and liabilities in each component fund, ORSA adequacy evaluation, retakāful/reinsurance cover and its security, assessment of Sharīʻah governance effectiveness, and attribution of cash flows between funds; inspection may be delegated to independent professionals provided the RSA retains effective oversight; follow-up frequency ranges from the next routine inspection (minor concerns) to frequent follow-ups (serious concerns), with use of certain powers depending on breach of a trigger level - most commonly the Prescribed Capital Requirement (paras 43, 45, 50, fn 14)

Enforcement powers should at least include: directions to reinforce financial position (requiring risk mitigation, capital increase, restricting/suspending dividends, restricting own-share purchase, and similar actions at the level of a PRF); restrictions on business (prohibiting new policies, withholding approvals, restricting asset transfers and subsidiaries); arranging transfer of obligations to another TU/RTU; suspending or revoking the licence; and barring individuals (para 52)

The RSA should have power to replace or restrict BOD members, senior management, key control functions, significant owners and external auditors, and to replace or require replacement of Sharīʿah board members, based on justified decision and reasonable grounds, subject to due process including appropriate rights of appeal; sanctions should be proportionate to the identified breach (paras 53-54)

Corporate governance: no 'single model' fits all takāful/retakāful models; fit-and-proper suitability for BOD, senior management and key control functions at first appointment and on an ongoing basis; the BOD is ultimately responsible for the effectiveness of its Sharīʻah board and implementation of its fatwas/Sharīʻah resolutions; participants' interests may diverge from shareholders' - e.g. a TO may be tempted to maximise contribution income to benefit from wakalah fees even if business is unprofitable for the PRF; IFSB-8 recommended a Governance Committee (paras 60, 64, 66-67)

Sharīʻah governance per IFSB-10 comprises ex-ante processes (issuance of pronouncements/resolutions and compliance checks before product offering) and ex-post processes (internal Sharīʻah review and Sharīʻah governance reporting); even where RSAs take no positions on substantive Shariah issues they should verify the Sharīʻah board is knowledgeable and independent; where a pronouncement is valid for a limited period or specified circumstances (e.g. permission to use conventional reinsurance based on dharurah), procedures must exist for review at period end (paras 70-71, 74, fn 19)

Takāful operational framework: the RSA must understand segregation of funds and examine how SHF/PRF/PIF segregation is maintained; contract clauses allowing the TO/RTO to vary the model or charges (e.g. wakalah fees) must have been fully presented to and approved by the Sharī'ah board; some RSAs issue guidelines on maximum allowable fee structure or fee calculation mechanism; fee structures including profit sharing (e.g. from investments under a muḍarabah agreement) and performance incentives must be specified in contracts and Sharīʻah-board approved (paras 80-83)

Cash-flow attribution policy must cover contributions, retakāful payments, fees, commissions, brokerage, recoveries and surplus distribution; claims-handling costs, business acquisition costs and brokerage fees offer particular scope for manipulation; the policy must be documented, approved by the BOD after Shari'ah board review and approval, and periodically reviewed; for retakāful cessions the policy covers outflows (contributions, wakālah fees) and inflows (ceding commission, profit commission, brokerage, recoveries, surplus distribution) (paras 84, 122)

IFSB-11 premises: increase likelihood of meeting contractual obligations; act as an early warning system for regulatory intervention; provide a buffer limiting participant loss and systemic effects; foster public confidence - complemented by IFSB-11's seven Key Principles; due to fund segregation, assets, liabilities and risks must be considered at the level of each fund, taking account of inter-fund relationships such as any commitment to provide qarḍ (paras 85-86)

Technical provisions must be set separately for each PRF with a properly documented basis per class of business and proper actuarial review; claims must be recorded as soon as received; retakāful provisioning needs particular scrutiny due to notification lag and volatility; Sharī'ah-compliant assets such as sukuk are often not traded in deep and liquid markets, raising valuation risk; RSAs should be alert to asset-liability mismatches by duration, currency or location (paras 88, 90, 92)

Financial or finite retakāful/reinsurance (FinRe) may enable a misleading presentation of financial strength; the absence of pooling and misalignment of form and substance generally render such arrangements non-Sharīʻah-compliant, and legitimate retakāful may be turned into FinRe by side letters or associated agreements; the Sharī`ah Board of the Islamic Development Bank does not consider FinRe arrangements Sharī`ah-compliant (para 93, fn 26)

Qarḍ and capital eligibility: where SHF capital is admissible as PRF resources via an earmarked qard facility, adequate unencumbered capital must exist in the SHF in addition to any stand-alone SHF solvency requirements; in a gone-concern/resolution situation it must be clear where the SHF's claim to qarḍ repayment ranks relative to participants' claims on the PRF and whether earmarked funds can meet other SHF liabilities (e.g. staff salaries), with clear documentation; capital recognised in more than one fund or entity requires adjustment (paras 96, 98-101)

Capital requirements follow IFSB-11's two solvency control levels: a risk-based Prescribed Capital Requirement (PCR) as trigger for supervisory intervention due to deteriorating financial strength, and a Minimum Capital Requirement as trigger for withdrawal of authorisation; internal models are not a significant sector feature and are not considered; the ORSA must cover at minimum underwriting, credit, market, operational and liquidity risks, Sharīʻah non-compliance risks and group risks, assess each fund (PRF, PIF, SHF) including qard transactions, analyse continuation over a three-to-five-year horizon, and include stress, scenario and reverse stress testing; the RSA may set an individual capital requirement covering PRF, SHF or both (paras 102-103, 113, 115-118)

Windows: takāful/retakāful windows must normally be completely separate from the conventional host in capital, accounts, profits and losses; the only exceptions passed to the host are the TO/RTO's share of profit as muḍārib and the management fee as wakil; RSAs should check policies preventing commingling, transparency of separation, and controls against channelling funds back to the conventional host; the host's ORSA should deal with the window separately subject to materiality (paras 129, 132-133)

Run-off: a formal run-off plan must cover current and forecast solvency of both PRF and SHF, impact on retakāful arrangements, treatment of qarḍ (including possible additional qarḍ), governance during run-off, and possible transfer of liabilities, and be subjected to Sharīʻah review; the RSA should have power to approve or refuse capital extraction and material outsourcing; transfer of resources from PRF to SHF is Sharīʻah-permissible only in three scenarios: (1) SHF recovering qarḍ provided to the PRF; (2) residual wakālah fee; (3) SHF share as muḍārib investing PRF funds (paras 147, 149, fn 31)
divergence_notes: On time-limited Sharīʻah pronouncements: 'An example might be permission to use conventional reinsurance rather than retakāful, based on arguments of dharurah' - indicating some Sharīʻah boards permit conventional reinsurance on necessity grounds (para 74, fn 19)

On financial/finite retakāful (FinRe): 'the absence of pooling and the misalignment of form and substance generally render such arrangements non-Sharīʻah-compliant' (para 93), with the footnote recording a specific institutional position: 'The Sharī`ah Board of the Islamic Development Bank does not consider financial, or finite risk, retakāful arrangements as Sharī`ah-compliant' (fn 26)

On Sharīʻah governance models: 'Given the different Sharīʻah governance structures and models that have been adopted in various jurisdictions, there is no "single model" or "one-size-fits-all" approach' (para 69)

On operating models across jurisdictions: the standard is written around the hybrid model but notes applicability 'with limited modifications to pure mutual models - as used, for example, in Sudan - and to the cooperative model used in Saudi Arabia' (para 15)
On fund segregation: 'This segregation may not be mandatory in the case of undertakings operating other than on the hybrid model' (para 62, fn 17)

standards.applicability: The assessment methodology is intended to apply to jurisdictions that have material Islamic capital markets; it is applicable to securities markets, intermediaries, information service providers (such as credit rating agencies) and products addressed by the CPICM (para 41). It does not apply to currency, bullion or physical commodity markets except to the extent that securities intermediaries deal for customers in such markets (para 43). The CPICM relating to the Regulator, Enforcement and Cooperation apply to all jurisdictions whether or not they have a market; other CPICM may not apply to some jurisdictions (para 58). CPICM 10 applies to regulators in jurisdictions where ICM players (issuers, fund managers, market intermediaries) explicitly claim Sharī'ah compliance of their offerings (para 242), including products with implicit claims such as an 'Amānah Fund' (para 248). Issuer CPICM 17-19 apply to public offerings and listed/publicly traded securities but not to the issuing of debt by government or statutory entities backed by government guarantee (para 377); CPICM 17 and 19 do not apply to sovereign ṣukūk, and CPICM 18 applies only to equity securities (para 382).
standards.structure: List of 38 Core Principles for Islamic Capital Market Regulation (CPICM) in groups A-J; Section 1: Introduction (background, premises/objectives, general approach, objectives of ICM regulation, regulatory environment, scope of assessment methodology, assessment process and measures, paras 1-71); Section 2: Principle-by-Principle Analysis (each CPICM with Preamble, Scope, Key Issues, Key Questions, Explanatory Notes and Benchmarks graded Fully/Broadly/Partly/Not Implemented); Appendix (CPICM-IOSCO mapping table); Definitions. A. Principles Relating to the Regulator: CPICM 1 'The responsibilities of the Regulator should be clear and objectively stated' (IOSCO 1); CPICM 2 'The Regulator should be operationally independent and accountable in the exercise of its functions and powers' (IOSCO 2); CPICM 3 'The Regulator should have adequate powers, proper resources and the capacity to perform its functions and exercise its powers' (IOSCO 3); CPICM 4 'The Regulator should adopt clear and consistent regulatory processes' (IOSCO 4); CPICM 5 'The staff of the Regulator should observe the highest professional standards, including appropriate standards of confidentiality' (IOSCO 5); CPICM 6 'The Regulator should have or contribute to a process to identify, monitor, mitigate and manage systemic risk, appropriate to its mandate' (IOSCO 6); CPICM 7 'The Regulator should have or contribute to a process to review the perimeter of regulation regularly' (IOSCO 7); CPICM 8 'The Regulator should seek to ensure that conflicts of interest and misalignment of incentives are avoided, eliminated, disclosed or otherwise managed' (IOSCO 8). B. Self-Regulation: CPICM 9 'Where the regulatory system makes use of Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs) that exercise some direct oversight responsibility for their respective areas of competence, such SROs should be subject to the oversight of the Regulator and should observe standards of fairness and confidentiality when exercising powers and delegated responsibilities' (IOSCO 9). C. Sharī'ah Governance: CPICM 10 'The Regulator should require that Sharī'ah governance is upheld for all products, activities, services and/or institutions implicitly or explicitly claiming Sharī'ah compliance in the Islamic capital market' (No IOSCO equivalent). D. Enforcement: CPICM 11 'The regulator should have comprehensive inspection, investigation and surveillance powers' (IOSCO 10); CPICM 12 'The regulator should have comprehensive enforcement powers' (IOSCO 11); CPICM 13 'The regulatory system should ensure an effective and credible use of inspection, investigation, surveillance and enforcement powers and implementation of an effective compliance programme' (IOSCO 12). E. Cooperation: CPICM 14 'The Regulator should have authority to share both public and non-public information with domestic and foreign counterparts' (IOSCO 13); CPICM 15 'Regulators should establish information sharing mechanisms that set out when and how they will share both public and non-public information with their domestic and foreign counterparts' (IOSCO 14); CPICM 16 'The regulatory system should allow for assistance to be provided to foreign Regulators who need to make inquiries in the discharge of their functions and exercise of their powers' (IOSCO 15). F. Issuers: CPICM 17 'There should be full, accurate and timely disclosure of financial results, risk and other information, which is material to investors' decisions' (IOSCO 16); CPICM 18 'Holders of securities in a company should be treated in a fair and equitable manner' (IOSCO 17); CPICM 19 'Accounting standards used by issuers to prepare financial statements should be of a high and internationally acceptable quality' (IOSCO 18); CPICM 20 'Ṣukūk should be subject to specific disclosure requirements commensurate with their specific nature and risk characteristics and which provide sufficient disclosures and transparency in all aspects related to compliance with Sharī'ah requirements' (No IOSCO equivalent). G. Auditors, Credit Rating Agencies and Other Information Service Providers: CPICM 21 'Auditors should be subject to adequate levels of oversight' (IOSCO 19); CPICM 22 'Auditors should be independent of the issuing entity that they audit' (IOSCO 20); CPICM 23 'Audit standards should be of a high and internationally acceptable quality' (IOSCO 21); CPICM 24 'Credit rating agencies should be subject to adequate levels of oversight. The regulatory system should ensure that credit rating agencies whose ratings are used for regulatory purposes are subject to registration and ongoing supervision' (IOSCO 22); CPICM 25 'Other entities that offer investors analytical or evaluative services should be subject to oversight and regulation appropriate to the impact their activities have on the market or the degree to which the regulatory system relies on them' (IOSCO 23). H. Islamic Collective Investment Schemes: CPICM 26 'The regulatory system should set standards for the eligibility, governance, organisation and operational conduct of those who wish to market or operate an Islamic collective investment scheme' (IOSCO 24); CPICM 27 'The regulatory system should provide for rules governing the legal form and structure of Islamic collective investment schemes and the segregation and protection of client assets' (IOSCO 25); CPICM 28 'Regulation should require disclosure, as set forth under the CPICM for issuers, which is necessary to evaluate the suitability of an Islamic collective investment scheme for a particular investor and the value of the investor's interest in the scheme' (IOSCO 26); CPICM 29 'Regulation should ensure that there is a proper and disclosed basis for asset valuation and the pricing and the redemption of units in an Islamic collective investment scheme' (IOSCO 27). I. Market Intermediaries: CPICM 30 'Regulation should provide for minimum entry standards for market intermediaries' (IOSCO 29); CPICM 31 'There should be initial and ongoing capital and other prudential requirements for market intermediaries that reflect the risks that the intermediaries undertake' (IOSCO 30); CPICM 32 'Market intermediaries should be required to establish an internal function that delivers compliance with standards for internal organisation and operational conduct, with the aim of protecting the interests of clients and their assets and ensuring proper management of risk, through which management of the intermediary accepts primary responsibility for these matters' (IOSCO 31); CPICM 33 'There should be procedures for dealing with the failure of a market intermediary in order to minimise damage and loss to investors and to contain systemic risk' (IOSCO 32). J. Secondary and Other Markets: CPICM 34 'The establishment of trading systems including securities exchanges should be subject to regulatory authorisation and oversight' (IOSCO 33); CPICM 35 'There should be ongoing regulatory supervision of exchanges and trading systems, which should aim to ensure that the integrity of trading is maintained through fair and equitable rules that strike an appropriate balance between the demands of different market participants' (IOSCO 34); CPICM 36 'Regulation should promote transparency of trading' (IOSCO 35); CPICM 37 'Regulation should be designed to detect and deter manipulation and other unfair trading practices' (IOSCO 36); CPICM 38 'Regulation should aim to ensure the proper management of large exposures, default risk and market disruption' (IOSCO 37). IOSCO Principle 28 (hedge funds) and Principle 38 (clearing and settlement) omitted (para 12).
key_points: The CPICM provide a set of core principles for regulation and supervision of the Islamic capital market, complementing IOSCO's 'Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation and its Methodology' (May 2017), with objectives of a minimum international standard, protection of consumers through sound Sharī'ah-compliance claims, and enhancing ICM soundness and stability (para 9)

The IFSB Council approved preparation of Core Principles for Islamic Finance Regulation at its 21st meeting on 12 December 2012; banking-segment core principles were issued in April 2015; the ICM-segment standard (CPICM) and its working group were approved at the 27th Council meeting on 8 December 2015 (paras 5-6)

There are 38 CPICM: two new principles added versus IOSCO - CPICM 10 on Sharī'ah governance and CPICM 20 on ṣukūk issuance - while IOSCO Principle 28 (hedge funds) and Principle 38 (clearing and settlement) were omitted (paras 11-12)

Hedge funds were omitted because Sharī'ah restrictions on, for example, short selling and the use of derivatives make it generally impossible within the ICM to structure a hedge fund as commonly understood (para 12)

Text on stable net asset value money market funds was omitted for strong Sharī'ah reasons; variable net asset value funds are not impossible provided they adhere to Sharī'ah rules and principles (para 13)

The three core objectives of ICM regulation are: protecting investors; ensuring markets are fair, efficient and transparent; and reducing systemic risk, approached in ways recognising Islamic-finance specificities such as sound Sharī'ah-compliance claims (paras 17-19)

Investor protection covers misleading claims of Sharī'ah compliance, with additional guidelines for remedial processes and purification of income should incidents of Sharī'ah non-compliance occur (para 22)

Sharī'ah non-compliance risk is defined (per IFSB-1) as the risk arising from failure by IIFS to comply with the Sharī'ah rules and principles determined by the Sharī'ah board of the IIFS or the relevant body in the jurisdiction (fn 6)

Assessment ratings are Fully Implemented, Broadly Implemented, Partly Implemented, Not Implemented and Not Applicable, determined from affirmative answers to Key Questions per benchmarks, with assessors able to adjust by one category with clear explanation (paras 65-71)

A Sharī'ah governance system comprises Sharī'ah pronouncements/resolutions, their dissemination, an internal Sharī'ah compliance review/audit (with non-compliance recorded, reported, rectified or invalidated), and an external annual Sharī'ah compliance review; a competent Sharī'ah board comprises, in line with IFSB-10, three or more Sharī'ah scholars, an external Sharī'ah consultancy firm or an individual scholar (para 235)

Sharī'ah principles essentially require investments to be free from ribā (interest), gharar (excessive uncertainty), maysir (gambling), and involvement with prohibited businesses (liquor, pork, conventional insurance, etc.) (fn 46)

CPICM 10 requires screening/approval by a competent Sharī'ah board or conformance with centralised Sharī'ah standards, board competence and conflict-of-interest management, disclosures on material changes affecting compliance, specified remedial actions on change to Sharī'ah non-compliant status, and cooperation arrangements for cross-border activities given differing Sharī'ah interpretations (CPICM 10 Key Issues 1-6); implicit compliance signals such as naming a fund an 'Amānah Fund' bring a product within ICM regulation (para 248)

Sharī'ah scholars may be required to follow behavioural standards including protection of confidential information, codes of conduct, governance standards, and restrictions on the number and types of Sharī'ah boards they may sit on concurrently (para 246)
For record keeping, the FAQs to the IOSCO MMoU consider five years as the norm for maintenance of records (fn 58)
Since 2005 the IOSCO MMoU has been the mandatory global minimum standard for enforcement cooperation among securities regulators; there is currently no equivalent IFSB MMoU (paras 312, 338)

Under CPICM 16 the domestic regulator should be able to assist foreign regulators in obtaining reports from a competent Sharī'ah board/authority on whether the asset/project backing a cross-border security is Sharī'ah-compliant; if a new opinion is required the requesting authority reasonably bears the costs (CPICM 16 Key Question 1(d), fn 101)

Issuer principles do not apply to government/statutory debt backed by government guarantee or to sovereign ṣukūk; CPICM 18 applies only to equity securities; any division of shares into classes establishing priority in dividends or priority in liquidation will not be considered Sharī'ah-compliant (paras 377, 382, fn 125)

CPICM 20 requires ṣukūk disclosures covering the Sharī'ah board, Sharī'ah review process, any fatwā and its Sharī'ah basis, deficiencies in underlying assets, tradability or non-tradability, purification and compensation payments, the role of Sharī'ah in interpretation in default/enforcement/amendment/restructuring (including that courts not bound by Sharī'ah may apply national law), post-issuance Sharī'ah assessment arrangements, structure/flow of funds, use of proceeds, recourse sources, and obligor/originator liability parallel to the issuer's (CPICM 20 Key Issues 1-4)

Substantial-ownership disclosure thresholds vary among jurisdictions (e.g. 5% or 10%) as does timeliness (e.g. 7 or 10 calendar or business days); periodic financial information warrants an affirmative answer if made available at least semi-annually (paras 420, 400)

Under CPICM 24, CRA methodologies must be consistent and comparable across conventional and Islamic securities without neglecting Islamic specificities: ṣukūk representing debts only, as in murābaḥah ṣukūk, cannot be traded unless at par, whereas ṣukūk representing undivided ownership in assets can be traded at an agreed price; violation results in Sharī'ah non-compliance risk which must impact the rating, and neglect of these specificities results in defective ratings (para 487)

For ICIS: eligibility criteria include adequate knowledge of Islamic finance and ex-ante and ex-post Sharī'ah compliance monitoring systems (CPICM 26 Key Issues 1, 5); a third party should review the ICIS valuation process at least annually (CPICM 29 Key Issue 5); imposing fees or charges on redemption of ICIS units is not Sharī'ah-compliant unless imposed for a specific service provided to the unitholder (fn 247); disclosures should cover Sharī'ah review and governance, treatment of tainted assets or income, and zakāh or other Sharī'ah-related obligatory payments per IFSB-19 paras 139-153 (para 574)

Market intermediaries claiming Sharī'ah compliance must have systems (controls, policies and procedures) ensuring compliance with Sharī'ah principles (para 594); entry standards require demonstrated knowledge of Islamic finance and Sharī'ah principles plus Sharī'ah governance per CPICM 10 (CPICM 30 Key Issue 2); internal organisation includes internal Sharī'ah audit and internal Sharī'ah compliance functions and controls for continuing compliance with Sharī'ah board rulings (CPICM 32 Key Issue 4, Key Question 1(b)); intermediaries must provide client statements at least annually (CPICM 32 Key Question 19)

For exchanges, principal, settlement, guarantee or performance risk can be assumed through a takāful fund/scheme, on a tabarru' basis without stipulating it as a condition, or by the exchange acting as third-party guarantor (kafīl) assuming risks without any counter-value, with liability in cases of negligence or misconduct (fn 309); high-speed algorithmic trading systems may commit Sharī'ah prohibitions, in particular the principle that a person should not sell securities he does not possess (fn 316); where a regulator lacks withdrawal authority, demonstrating authority to suspend all trading for at least six months can support a Partly Implemented rating (para 677)

Under CPICM 38, margin is considered as a trust held by the exchange or clearing house that can only be utilised in cases of default, negligence or misconduct, and shall be returned to its owner once he finally exits the market; Sharī'ah-compliant guarantees by the central bank are among mechanisms for addressing financial failure (paras 717, 729)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: an exchange may assume principal, settlement, guarantee or performance risk through a takāful fund/scheme, on a tabarru' (donation) basis without stipulating it as a condition, or by acting as a third-party guarantor (kafīl) 'assuming these risks without any counter-value' - i.e. gratuitously - though liable in cases of negligence or misconduct; kafālah is defined as a contract where the guarantor conjoins the guaranteed party in assuming the latter's specified liability, and ṣukūk featuring kafālah/guarantee require additional disclosure parallel to conventional requirements.
clauses: fn 309 (CPICM 34): 'the exchange would act as a third-party guarantor or a kafīl, assuming these risks without any counter-value. However, in cases of negligence or misconduct the exchange will be held liable.'
CPICM 20 Key Issue 1: additional or varied disclosure requirements where the ṣukūk has features such as 'kafālah/guarantee, redemption options, convertibility, exchangeability and subordination'
Definitions: Kafālah - 'A contract where the guarantor conjoins the guaranteed party in assuming the latter's specified liability.'

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: ṣukūk or securitised exposures that represent debts only are not tradable except at par - 'if it represents debts only, as in the case of murābaḥah ṣukūk, it cannot be traded unless at par; whereas if it represents shares of undivided ownership in assets, it can be traded based on an agreed-upon price between the two parties'; violation of these characteristics results in Sharī'ah non-compliance risk which must impact the credit rating.
clauses: para 487 (CPICM 24): murābaḥah ṣukūk 'cannot be traded unless at par'; asset-ownership ṣukūk tradable at agreed price; 'Violation of such characteristics would result in Sharī'ah non-compliance risk, which must in turn impact on the rating.'

key_points: Aims to specify key principles and practices for IIFS banking-segment disclosures to achieve transparency and promote market discipline, introducing harmonised templates for quantitative disclosure of key risks (paras 8, 12)

Updates IFSB-4 in line with four BCBS publications: Pillar 3 consolidated and enhanced framework (March 2017), Revised Pillar 3 (January 2015), Pillar 3 updated-framework consultative document (February 2018) and Technical Amendment on accounting provisions (March 2018) (para 13)

Applies to Islamic banks, Islamic funds managed by IIFS as restricted investment accounts, and Islamic windows of conventional banks; fully consolidated at holding company level or individual basis at RSA discretion; not for groups consisting of non-IIFS entities (paras 13-14)
IFSB-4 is not rendered invalid for jurisdictions that are not implementing Basel III; BCBS adaptations only where not in conflict with Shari'ah rules and principles (para 15)
Implementation from end-2020; Templates 15, 19, 20 and Tables 19-20 with Templates 29-32 from 1 January 2022; Template 27 LCR from 1 January 2015; Template 28 NSFR from 1 January 2018 (para 16)

Six disclosure principles: formal BOD-approved disclosure policy; clear; comprehensive; meaningful to users; consistent over time; comparable across IIFS; a Governance Committee overseeing IAH issues is recommended (paras 29-39, fn 6)

Materiality is a qualitative use test based on user information needs and Shari'ah requirements; disclosures published in a stand-alone document with the same assurance level as financial reporting; requirements applied on a comply-or-explain basis (paras 18, 20-21, 43)

Signposting to a separate document permitted only if content is equivalent, same consolidation scope, disclosure is mandatory, and assurance level is equivalent or greater (paras 22-24); reporting frequencies vary between quarterly, semi-annual and annual, published concurrently with financial reports (paras 25-26)

Template 1 key prudential metrics reported quarterly with previous four quarters (T to T-4), including CET1/tier 1/total capital, CCB requirement (2.5% from 2019), leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR, total UPSIA and RPSIA funds, PER shareholders' and IAH components, and IRR balance (paras 46-49, Template 1)

RWA funded by PSIA in principle excluded from the CAR denominator, but a proportion alpha is included to reflect DCR; alpha has two components (UPSIA and RPSIA) where smoothing extends to restricted PSIA; the applicable alpha, the assets to which it applies and the application policy must be disclosed (para 50, fn 17)

Template 2 RWA overview: row 15 deducts PSIA-funded credit/market RWA, row 17 applies (1-alpha) to UPSIA-funded RWA and row 18 applies alpha to RWA funded by PER and IRR of UPSIA; totals follow IFSB-15 paras 285(a)/(b); column (c) minimum capital should equal 8% of RWA; floor adjustment after transitional cap limits RWA increase to 25% (paras 51-52, Template 2, Table 2 row 21)

Unrestricted IAH are in principle a type of equity investor (rabb al-mal under the mudarabah contract), not creditors; supervisory practice of treating them like conventional depositors with a smoothed market-reflecting return is generally not considered Shari'ah-compliant (fn 12)

Template 3 composition of regulatory capital (semi-annual) includes a zakah obligations adjustment, assessed when the IIFS has been in operation for at least 12 months; deduction thresholds of 10% and 15% apply to investments in financial/takaful entities, residential financing servicing rights and deferred tax assets (para 54, Template 3, Table 3 rows 7, 18-22)

IsDB Group Shari'ah Board opinion: partial or full write-down of any capital instrument violates Shari'ah rules and principles; conversion must be subject to Shari'ah-compliant parameters; Shari'ah-compliant payment hierarchy gives priority to secured creditors (to collateral value) and to IAH (to value of assets financed by their funds, held as trust not debt), with remaining creditors ranking pro-rata without priority (fns 21-22)

CCB of 2.5% CET1 sits above minima of 4.5% CET1 and 8% total capital; Template 6 disclosure of CET1 ratios triggering capital distribution constraints, illustrated with triggers of 9% (4.5%+2.5%+2% CCyB) and 10% (adding 1% CET1 used for the 6% tier 1 minimum) against an actual 12% CET1 ratio (paras 64-68, Templates 6, Table 5)

Three-step reconciliation links the published balance sheet to regulatory capital: report both consolidation scopes, expand and reference balance-sheet elements, and map them to Template 3; Templates 8-9 map financial statement categories to regulatory risk categories with qualitative explanations (paras 69-78, Templates 7-9, Table 6)

Section 4 IAH disclosures: IAH provide funding as rabb al-mal on a profit-sharing and loss-bearing mudarabah basis; requirements also apply to musharakah-based accounts with no actual or constructive capital protection or promised returns; PER/IRR movements disclosed separately for UPSIA and RPSIA if kept separately; per GN-3 para 28, IAH give up rights to PER/IRR on terminating their relationship on the basis of mubara'ah (paras 79-82, fn 30)

Retail investor-oriented disclosures in plain language must cover mudarib share as a percentage of total investment profit and extent of waiver, PER/IRR appropriation and smoothing rights, withdrawal rights and penalties, possibility of full or partial loss of principal, and must not contain projections; any commitment to keep IAH capital intact must not be contractual as that would not be Shari'ah-compliant; historical returns over past three to five years and average rates by 3-, 6-, 12- and 36-month maturity are disclosed (paras 85-90, Tables 7-9, fn 33)

Credit risk: capital impairment risk on non-traded mudarabah/musharakah equity is treated as part of credit risk; Template 15 breaks exposures down by risk weight per asset class (e.g. sovereigns 0-150%, banks 20-150%, sukuk 10-150%, equity exposures under profit-sharing modes 100%/150%/250%/400%, retail 45%/75%/100%, bands up to 1250%); defaulted exposures are the unsecured portion past due more than 90 days; penalties imposed on customers for default and disposition of such monies must be disclosed (paras 94-97, Templates 15-16, Tables 11-12, Table 11 item 17)

Per Shari'ah rules it is not permissible to restructure by increasing the debt; CRM disclosures cover hamish jiddiyyah (refundable security deposit with limited recourse taken before contract) and urbun (earnest money after contract), Shari'ah-compliant equities, ICIS units, sukuk and third-party guarantees with the guarantor's risk weight (fn 48, fns 50-51, Table 15)

LCR disclosed quarterly as simple averages of daily observations over the previous quarter (typically 90 days) with unweighted, weighted and adjusted values; NSFR disclosed semi-annually on a consolidated basis with ASF/RSF by residual maturity buckets (no maturity, <6 months, 6 months to <1 year, >=1 year); both adapted from GN-6 (paras 121-135, Templates 27-28)

Operational risk definition includes Shari'ah non-compliance risk; Template 30 requires 10 years of historical losses using EUR 20,000 and EUR 100,000 thresholds, applicable to IIFS with BI above EUR 1bn (or with supervisory permission); BIC marginal coefficients are 12% for BI <= EUR 1bn, 15% for EUR 1bn-30bn, 18% for BI > EUR 30bn; PIDC component capped at 2.25% of profit-earning assets; ILM equals one where jurisdictions exclude losses (paras 139-145, Templates 30-32, Tables 21-23)

Rate of return risk (analogue of interest rate risk in the banking book) is disclosed via changes in EVE and NIFS under six benchmark shock scenarios (parallel up/down, steepener, flattener, short rate up/down); repricing in IIFS is possible only by linking ijarah rentals to a benchmark, other contracts being fixed-price; DCR section defines PER (appropriated from mudarabah profits before distribution, partly shareholders' equity and partly IAH equity) and IRR (from IAH profits after mudarib share, absorbing losses only); smoothing may also use unconditional mudarib-share reduction (via tabarru' by shareholder decision) or hibah from shareholders' income, and DCR policies are disclosed annually (paras 146-160, Template 33, fns 77-78, 82)

Shari'ah governance disclosures include the Shari'ah board's compliance opinion, independence statement per IFSB-10 paras 42-43, SNCI amounts and rectification, number of violations split between financing of non-compliant assets/activities and procedural lapses (Template 38), pronouncements issued in the last 12 months (recommended), charity account movements including sources such as SNCI and penalties (Template 39), aggregate Shari'ah board remuneration, and zakah calculation method and contributions; asset encumbrance treats assets financed by IAH funds (including commingled share) as encumbered; Islamic windows are defined as non-separate-legal-entity parts of conventional institutions, accounted for as virtual branches with a complete set of financial statements in the notes and full application of PSIA, smoothing, Shari'ah-governance and commingling disclosure requirements; deposit insurance disclosures must state whether each scheme is Shari'ah-compliant, maximum coverage per account type, and PSIA payout details (paras 152, 162-184, Tables 29-33, Templates 37-39)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: securitised exposures based on financial assets (cash and receivables) are not tradable, whereas those based on tangible assets or usufruct are tradable; murabahah and salam instruments are not tradable
clauses: fn 56: 'Securitisation exposures are of two types: (a) securitised exposures that are based on tangible assets or usufruct, which are tradable; and (b) securitised exposures that are based on financial assets (cash and receivables) which are not tradable.'
fn 58: 'Murabahah and salam instruments are not tradable.'

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: unilateral binding promise structures are accepted provided the promise remains separate from the contract - murabahah 'can be preceded by a promise to purchase'; ijarah 'could be preceded by a unilateral binding promise'; ijarah muntahiyah bittamlik uses 'a separate promise from the lessor giving the lessee a binding promise to own the asset'; in diminishing musharakah the buying partner 'is only allowed to promise to buy' and the buying/selling must not be stipulated in the partnership contract; compensation under hamish jiddiyyah is limited to the actual loss from non-fulfilment of the promise
clauses: Definitions: diminishing musharakah - 'The buying and selling is independent of the partnership contract and should not be stipulated in the partnership contract, since the buying partner is only allowed to promise to buy.'
Definitions: murabahah - 'The murabahah contract can be preceded by a promise to purchase from the customer.'
Definitions: ijarah muntahiyah bittamlik - 'a separate promise from the lessor giving the lessee a binding promise to own the asset at the end of the lease period'

fn 50 and Definitions: hamish jiddiyyah - seller has recourse 'to compensate him to the extent of the actual loss resulting from the reduction of the selling price to another party from the cost price'

divergence_notes: fn 12: certain supervisors require or permit IIFS to treat unrestricted IAH similarly to conventional depositors, paying a smoothed market-reflecting return without bearing losses - 'such a practice is generally not considered SharT'ah-compliant' (fn 12)

fn 21: the IsDB Group Shari'ah Board 'is of the opinion that the mechanism of partial or full write-down of any capital instrument is a mechanism that violates SharT'ah rules and principles'; its presence in the template is only to disclose such practices; conversion must be subjected to parameters that make it Shari'ah-compliant (fn 21)
fn 33: an IIFS's commitment to maintaining IAH capital intact 'should not be construed as a contractual commitment, as this would not be SharT'ah-compliant' (fn 33)
fn 48: 'According to SharT'ah rules and principles, it is not permissible to restructure by increasing the debt' (fn 48)

fn 68: 'Not all types of correlation/non-correlation trading portfolios are SharT'ah-compliant', and IIFS must follow guidelines of centralised Shari'ah boards in their jurisdictions where available, or obtain approval from their own Shari'ah boards (fn 68)

fn 77: 'The original SharT'ah ruling is that U/RIAH bear the risk of losses, and IIFS would not compensate them for that'; unconditional smoothing by forgoing profits 'from the SharT'ah perspective, is a pure hibah that is not binding' (fn 77)

para 171: jurisdictional divergence in Shari'ah governance - 'some countries have a centralised SharT'ah authority that issues or approves the applicable pronouncement/resolution', while in other countries the applicable resolution/pronouncement is issued by each IIFS's own Shari'ah board (para 171)

fn 94: a survey during the standard's development indicated 'several jurisdictions require IIFS to insure customer deposits and investment accounts, even in the absence of a SharT'ah-compliant deposit insurance scheme' (fn 94)

para 39: in cases of differences or conflicts between national regulatory frameworks and IFSB standards, supervisory authorities need to harmonise or resolve them 'without violating SharT'ah rules and principles' (para 39)

standards.applicability: Primarily banking institutions offering Islamic financial services: fully fledged Islamic commercial banks, Islamic investment banks/companies, Islamic banking subsidiaries of conventional banks, Islamic windows (branches/divisions/units) of conventional banks, and other institutions determined by the supervisory authority (para 8); applied on a fully consolidated basis at holding-company level within an IIFS group/subgroup, on a solo basis, or both, as the RSA determines; not intended to apply at consolidated level to groups containing non-IIFS entities; application should be proportionate to nature, size and complexity (para 9). standards.structure: Seven sections plus Definitions and Appendices A-C: Section 1 General Considerations (paras 1-15: introduction; purpose/objectives; scope; implementation date; specificities of Islamic financial instruments; structure). Section 2 Capital Adequacy and Macroprudential Measures (paras 16-103: CAR requirement; standard and supervisory-discretion CAR formulas; capital conservation buffer; countercyclical buffer; leverage ratio; D-SIBs; Islamic window operations). Section 3 Regulatory Capital (paras 104-117: CET1, AT1, Tier 2 criteria; treatment of PSIA, PER and IRR; regulatory adjustments/deductions). Section 4 Principles for Minimum Capital Requirements (paras 118-416: credit risk incl. exposures under profit-sharing modes and CRM techniques; market risk (trading book, valuation, simplified standardised approach); operational risk (standardised approach, loss data, SNCR); PSIA, smoothing, DCR and determination of alpha). Section 5 Capital Requirements for Islamic Financing and Investment Assets (paras 417-584: murabahah/MPO; commodity murabahah; salam; istisna; ijarah/IMB; musharakah and diminishing musharakah; mudarabah; qard; wakalah bi al-istithmar, each with stage-by-stage summary tables). Section 6 Treatment of Exposures Related to Sukuk (paras 585-676: securitisation process, true sale, SPE, derecognition, per-structure sukuk RWs, retained exposures). Section 7 Real Estate Activities (paras 677-705). Definitions. Appendix A: Business indicator components. Appendix B: Operational guidelines for the countercyclical buffer. Appendix C: Factors in determining D-SIBs.
key_points: Recommended implementation date for the Standard across jurisdictions is 1 January 2023 (para 10)

CAR = total capital / total RWA (credit + market + operational risks); at all times CET1 >=4.5% of RWA, Tier 1 (CET1+AT1) >=6%, total capital >=8%; component minimums CET1 >=4.5%, AT1 >=1.5%, Tier 2 >=2% (paras 17-18, Table 2)
Standard formula: absent smoothing, RWAs funded by PSIA (credit + market, incl. PER/IRR balances) are deducted from the CAR denominator, leaving operational risk (para 20, fn 6)

Supervisory discretion formula: denominator deducts RWA funded by restricted PSIA, plus (1 - alpha) x RWA funded by unrestricted PSIA, plus alpha x RWA funded by PER and IRR of unrestricted PSIA (para 20)

Alpha is the proportion of UPSIA-funded RWA included in the denominator due to DCR from smoothing; value near 0 = investment-like product, near 1 = deposit-like; set at supervisory discretion using the IFSB GN-4 (March 2011) methodology (paras 408, 414-416)

Capital conservation buffer of 2.5% of RWAs in CET1 only, giving CET1+CCB of 7%; minimum capital conservation ratios: 100% of profits conserved at CET1 4.5-5.125%, 80% at >5.125-5.75%, 60% at >5.75-6.375%, 40% at >6.375-7%, 0% above 7% (paras 23, 30, Table 1)

Countercyclical buffer of 0-2.5% of RWAs in CET1 (can be set higher domestically; international reciprocity only up to 2.5%); increases announced up to 12 months before implementation, releases take effect immediately; operated via credit-to-GDP gap with Hodrick-Prescott smoothing parameter 400,000, buffer zero below gap L=2%, rising linearly to VBmax=2.5% at H=10% (paras 43-44, fn 9, Appendix B para 3)

Leverage ratio = Tier 1 capital / exposure measure >=3%, calculated as the average of the monthly ratio over the quarter; assets funded by RPSIA excluded, UPSIA-funded assets included unless the RSA exercises national discretion; Shari'ah-compliant hedging exposure per SA-CCR; OIC Fiqh Academy resolution 238 (9/24) binds hedging instruments (paras 54, 65-67)

D-SIBs require higher loss absorbency met fully by CET1, indicatively 0.5-3.5% of RWAs above minimum and buffers; assessment factors: size, interconnectedness, substitutability, complexity, country-specific factors (paras 89-91, Appendix C)

AT1 capital is issued as mudarabah sukuk commingled with the CET1 pool (mudarabah replaces IFSB-15's musharakah choice so non-distribution is not default), perpetual, no step-ups, callable only after five years with supervisory approval, and mandatorily convertible to common shares at an RSA trigger of a CET1 ratio of at least 5.125% or at non-viability/public-sector injection (paras 110-111, fn 30)

Tier 2 capital is gone-concern, debt-creating subordinated sukuk (not mudarabah/wakalah, fn 36) with original maturity of at least five years, straight-line amortisation in the last five years, callable after five years; general provisions in Tier 2 limited to 1.25 percentage points of credit RWAs under the standardised approach (paras 112-115)

PSIA are not regulatory capital; all IRR and the IAH portion of PER belong to IAH equity (para 116); CET1 deductions include goodwill/intangibles, DTAs, treasury shares, pension fund net assets, securitisation gain-on-sale; retained residual equity in securitisation is risk-weighted 1,250%; investments >10% of common shares in banking/financial/takaful entities are fully deducted via the corresponding deduction approach; zakah obligations assessed after 12 months of operation (para 117)

Credit risk uses ECRA (rated jurisdictions) or SCRA: sovereigns 0/20/50/100/150% and 100% unrated (Table 3); listed MDBs incl. Islamic Development Bank 0% (para 137), other MDBs 20-150% or 50% unrated (Table 5); banks/IIFS SCRA Grades A/B/C = 40/75/150% (30% possible if counterparty CET1 >=14% and Tier 1 leverage >=5%), short-term 20/50/150% (Table 7, fn 63); sovereign RW floor for transfer/convertibility risk (para 155)

Corporates: rated 20/50/75/100/150%, unrated 100%; in no-ratings jurisdictions 100% with 65% for investment-grade corporates and 85% for unrated corporate SMEs (annual sales <=EUR 50m); regulatory retail 75% (aggregate exposure <=EUR 1m and <=0.2% of portfolio), transactors 45%, other retail 100%; specialised financing 130% pre-operational / 100% operational / 80% high-quality operational when unrated (paras 158-174, Table 9)

Real estate financing: RRE by FTV 20/25/30/40/50/70% (Table 10); income-producing RRE 30-105% (Table 11); CRE min(60%, counterparty RW) or counterparty RW (Table 12), income-producing CRE 70/90/110% (Table 13); 150% where para 178 requirements unmet and repayment is property-cash-flow dependent; 1.5x RW multiplier (capped at 150%) for unhedged currency-mismatched retail/RRE exposures (paras 179-191)

Profit-sharing (musharakah/mudarabah) banking-book exposures use the simple risk-weight method: 250% for commercial-enterprise/listed equity investments, 400% for unlisted/short-term unlisted equity, 100% for legislated-programme holdings up to 10% of Tier 1+Tier 2; ICIS equity via look-through, mandate-based (1.2x if external data) or fall-back approach at 1,250%; diminishing musharakah and musharakah with ijarah/murabahah subcontracts look through to counterparty RW (100% unrated) plus 100% on ijarah residual value (paras 204-215)

Defaulted exposure = past due more than 90 days or defaulted counterparty; RW 150% where specific provisions <20% of outstanding, 100% where >=20% (RSA discretion 50% where >=50%); RRE-secured defaulted 100% (50% discretionary); other assets 100%, cash and allocated gold bullion 0%, cash items in collection 20% (paras 216-219, Table 14)

CRM: eligible mitigants include hamish jiddiyah (binding PP/PL only; refundable HJ under non-binding promise is not eligible), urbun, third-party guarantees (irrevocable, unconditional; guarantor A- minimum for corporates), pledged assets (rahn), leased assets as quasi-collateral, and netting against deposits/PSIA; comprehensive approach E* = max[0, E(1+He) - C(1-Hc-Hfx)] with 8% currency-mismatch haircut, physical collateral haircut >=30%; maturity mismatch Pa = P x (t-0.25)/(T-0.25), CRM with residual maturity under one year (or under three months) not recognised (paras 246-276, Tables 16-17)

Market risk simplified standardised approach: MCR = CRPR x 1.30 + CREQ x 3.50 + CRFX x 1.20 + CRC&I x 1.90; equity specific and general risk 8% each; sukuk specific risk 0-12% by category/tenor and general risk by 13 time bands 0-6%; FX charge 8% of overall net open position with gold and silver under FX per the Shari'ah spot-exchange rule (fn 135); commodities simplified approach 15% net + 3% gross (maturity ladder: 1.5% spread rate, 0.6% carry surcharge, 15% net); inventory 15%; exemption if FX business <=100% of capital and net open position <=2% (paras 314-357, Tables 18-23)

Operational risk uses the single standardised approach replacing IFSB-15's BIA/SA/ASA: BIC marginal coefficients 12% (BI <=EUR 1bn), 15% (EUR 1-30bn), 18% (>EUR 30bn); ORC = BIC x ILM where LC = 15 x average annual losses over 10 years (minimum 5 years transitional); ILM = 1 for bucket 1; loss inclusion threshold EUR 20,000 (RSA may raise to EUR 100,000 for buckets 2-3); operational-risk RWA = 12.5 x ORC; SNCR (failure of Shari'ah governance and fiduciary risk as mudarib/wakil/musharik) and cyber and legal risk are operational-risk categories (paras 358-379, fn 157)

Islamic windows: RSAs may require separate window capital and CAR alongside consolidated requirements; where a separate window CAR is calculated without consolidation, the window's required capital is deducted from the parent's common equity; where no separate requirement, UPSIA risk absorbency is recognised via the alpha factor; the Shari'ah board encourages conversion of windows into legally separate Islamic institutions (paras 97-101, fn 22)

Per-contract charges (Section 5): murabahah/non-binding MPO asset in possession 15% capital charge (187.5% RW), receivables at obligor RW (100% unrated); binding MPO credit exposure = acquisition cost less asset market value (net of haircut) less HJ; CMT (CMLF/CMF) exposure = acquisition cost less commodity value, counterparty RW thereafter; salam counterparty RW with no salam/parallel-salam offsetting of credit exposures, simplified market charge 15% net + 3% gross; istisna unbilled WIP without parallel istisna adds 1.6% (20% RW) market charge, own-account WIP 15%; ijarah/IMB lease receivables at lessee RW less recovery value of leased asset, operating-ijarah residual value 100% RW and 15% charge on carrying value after lease expiry; qard at borrower RW (100% unrated); wakalah business ventures 250% listed / 400% unlisted (paras 437-584, Tables 25-40)

Sukuk/securitisation: originator may derecognise securitised assets only on true sale, bankruptcy remoteness, no effective control, SPE transferee, and clean-up calls exercisable only when 10% or less of purchase consideration remains (para 616); 1,250% RW where the IIFS cannot perform required due diligence (para 631); retained securitisation exposures risk-weighted 20/50/100/350/1,250% by rating with B+ and below or unrated at 1,250% (Table 41, paras 675-676); eligible liquidity facilities 50% CCF (100% if the facility rating is used); servicer qard cash advances may be 0% at national discretion (paras 671-672); per-structure RWs: salam sukuk at supplier RW, istisna sukuk without parallel istisna 100% plus 20% price-risk add-on, IMB sukuk at lessee RW, murabahah sukuk at obligor RW and non-tradable (paras 639-666)

Real estate: direct investment exposures 187.5% RW (equivalent to a 15% capital charge), including holdings in the non-binding stage (para 701); investment via joint venture/equity participation 400% unlisted or 300% listed (para 691); investment in a real estate subsidiary above 15% of regulatory capital 1,250%, below the threshold not lower than 100% (para 692); real estate investment activities suitable only on a very limited scale (para 689)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: a third-party undertaking to make good impairment losses must be a free-of-charge Shari'ah-compliant undertaking (kafalah for debts or a promise to donate), 'since accepting a third-party undertaking for a fee is not Shariah-compliant unless the fee is based on actual and direct costs' (fn 97); sukuk credit enhancement by a third party is given 'without any consideration being received by the third party', with recourse to the obligor permitted only under kafalah, not under a donation-form undertaking (para 610); guarantees used as CRM are given 'without any consideration being received by the guarantor' (para 250)

IFSB: in some jurisdictions reverse CMT- or tawarruq-based funding is the primary funding source for IIFS 'despite the differing opinions of the Shariah scholars on this mechanism' (para 50); reverse CMT-based deposits are a form of leverage which, together with CMT-based term financing, 'has the potential to create unlimited debt in the system' (para 51); nonetheless the standard provides full capital treatment for CMLF/CMF per IFSB GN-2 (paras 442-451); CMLF is strictly a receivable and 'should not be classified as an investment' (fn 172)

IFSB: sukuk based on receivables are not tradable and cannot be used to issue sukuk on their own; they may be combined with non-financial assets in a pool provided the non-financial proportion is not less than an acceptable minimum ratio, but combining separate monetary and non-monetary portfolios merely to justify tradability 'is not considered Shariah-compliant' (para 614); murabahah sukuk, 'being receivables, are not tradable from a Shariah perspective' (para 665); salam sukuk are non-tradable as the subject matter is a receivable (para 639); istisna sukuk tradability where value is paid in cash in parallel istisna 'will be subject to the rules of dealing with debt' (para 643); trading in sukuk 'does not involve trading in debt' listed among differences from conventional finance (para 221)

IFSB: gold, silver and currency fall under foreign exchange risk 'in accordance with the Shariah rules and principles that require the exchange of different currencies to be made on the basis of spot exchange', unlike BCBS which treats gold as FX for volatility reasons and silver as a commodity (fn 135); derivative contracts such as options or futures 'are not deemed Shariah-compliant' (para 318); the IFSB Shariah board resolves that IIFS must abide by OIC Fiqh Academy resolution no. 238 (9/24) on Shariah-compliant hedging, while exposures in contravening instruments in permissive jurisdictions must still be recognised prudentially under SA-CCR (para 67); OTC hedging and cash-flow hedge reserves are repeatedly flagged as contravening that resolution (fns 88, 90, 43, 115)

IFSB: a binding promise to sell equities or sukuk 'is not considered a contract' from a Shariah perspective and hence is not short selling nor a derivative, but RSAs may prudentially treat it as a short position attracting a capital charge (para 318, fn 131); the classification and distinctions between a non-binding and a binding MPO 'are subject to the criteria and opinions set out by the respective Shariah Supervisory Board of the IIFS' (para 421); in a binding MPO the customer's promise is enforceable, HJ recourse is limited to actual loss, and absent proper documentation and legal enforceability the asset reverts to non-binding (price-risk) treatment (paras 425, 429-432); a diminishing-musharakah partner 'gives a binding promise in a separate document' to buy out the IIFS's share (para 205); an agreement to lease 'may be considered as a promise to lease, depending on the applicable Shariah interpretations' (para 505)

divergence_notes: 'The Shariah rules and principles mentioned for explanatory purposes in the Standard do not encompass all the practices followed by IIFS in different jurisdictions' - IIFS must fulfil requirements of their own supervisors and Shariah boards (para 15)
On indicative Shariah requirements for financing contracts: 'The list is neither exhaustive nor conclusive and may vary according to the views of different Shariah boards' (para 393)

On true sale criteria for sukuk: 'From a juristic perspective, subject to jurists' interpretations in the jurisdiction, there are four key criteria for a transaction to be considered as a true sale' (para 601)

Some wakalah-based deposit contracts constructed with fixed return and/or capital guarantee are 'not considered Shariah-compliant' per an IFSB survey, making them closer to deposits than PSIA (fn 163)

Where a jurisdiction permits hedging instruments 'which contravenes the resolution of the OIC Fiqh Academy, which the Shariah board is of the opinion must be adhered to', the exposure is still recognised prudentially in line with SA-CCR (para 67)

The Shariah board opines that asset-based sukuk may only be issued in a Shariah-compliant manner subject to conditions on beneficial ownership, and that recourse should be to the underlying assets rather than the originator except for sovereign sukuk (fns 190-191); if ownership and risks are not transferred to sukuk holders the sukuk 'will not be considered Shariah-complaint' regardless of asset-backed/asset-based labels (fn 204)

Priority of claims differs: 'The claim should be documented with a collateral (rahn); only then, would it have priority. Otherwise, there should be no priority between claims' (fn 102, fn 105); tranching with preferential treatment among sukuk holders 'is not permissible from a Shariah perspective' (fn 192)
