standards.applicability: Applies to ICM products, including but not limited to sukuk, ICIS and Shari'ah-compliant equities, and to market intermediaries operating in the ICM ('firms'), particularly those interfacing with clients: brokers, asset managers, portfolio managers, investment advisers, firms offering/recommending/selling investment products, executing or transmitting orders, market making and underwriting, placing of financial instruments, multilateral trading facilities, crypto-asset platforms, P2P financing platforms, equity crowdfunding platforms, and online retail trading and investment platforms such as robo-advisers (para 8). Crypto-asset provisions apply only to security tokens in category (iv) of the Annex taxonomy approved by the relevant Shari'ah boards; other crypto categories are the subject of Shari'ah debate and out of scope (paras 9-10). RSAs should apply proportionality per the nature, scale and complexity of intermediaries and markets (para 12). Short selling and derivatives are not a feature of the ICM for Shari'ah reasons and are not addressed (para 5). Securities exchanges, clearing and settlement, and corporate governance of issuers are not covered (addressed in CPIFR) (para 16). Level of implementation may depend on a jurisdiction's general legal framework (para 18).
standards.structure: Section 1: Introduction - 1.1 Background (paras 1-5), 1.2 Objectives (paras 6-7), 1.3 Scope of Application (paras 8-12), 1.4 Approach of the Standard (paras 13-16), 1.5 Implementation Date (paras 17-18). Section 2: The Guiding Principles, 17 principles under 8 headings: 2.1 General Principles of Investor Protection - Principle 1 'Regulators should require that market intermediaries operating in the Islamic capital market act honestly, fairly and professionally in accordance with the best interests of investors' (paras 19-27); 2.2 Compliance with Shari'ah Principles - Principle 2 'There should be appropriate policies, procedures, resources, systems and controls in place for Shari'ah governance if a firm offers products or services that make an implicit or explicit claim of Shari'ah compliance' (paras 28-40); 2.3 Product Governance - Principle 3 'Measures to protect investors should be adapted to the particularities of defined categories of investors' (paras 41-50); Principle 4 'Where firms offer Shari'ah-compliant financial instruments to clients... products are designed to meet the needs of an identified target market... undergo appropriate Shari'ah and product approval processes, and... distributed to the identified target market' (paras 51-63); Principle 5 'Regulators may undertake temporary product intervention measures where a product claimed as Shari'ah-compliant creates a significant investor protection concern' (paras 64-68); 2.4 Disclosure and Transparency - Principle 6 'A robust disclosure regime for Shari'ah-compliant equities should be in place to promote transparency... and protect minority investors' (paras 69-78); Principle 7 'Where equities are labelled as Shari'ah-compliant by, or on behalf of, an RSA or exchange, there should be adequate disclosures relating to the Shari'ah-screening methodology... a regular review... and sufficient disclosures regarding any change in an equity's Shari'ah-compliant status' (paras 79-85); Principle 8 'Intermediaries in the Islamic capital market should be required to provide appropriate information in good time to clients... as well as the mechanisms in place for Shari'ah governance where a claim of Shari'ah compliance is made' (paras 86-106); 2.5 Conduct of Business - Principle 9 (suitability/appropriateness) 'adequate policies and procedures... to understand the essential facts and characteristics about their clients, including their preference for Shari'ah-compliant investments' (paras 107-137); Principle 10 (fit and proper) 'natural persons giving investment advice or providing investment or ancillary services... possess the necessary knowledge and competence' (paras 138-153); Principle 11 'Senior management and the board of directors... should collectively possess the necessary knowledge and competence' (paras 154-161); Principle 12 (best execution) 'take all sufficient steps to obtain the best possible result for their clients, taking into account... any considerations necessary to ensure Shari'ah compliance' (paras 162-174); Principle 13 (marketing and promotion) 'All information, including marketing communications... shall be fair, clear and not misleading' (paras 175-183); Principle 14 (conflicts of interest) 'effective policies and procedures to identify actual or potential conflicts of interest, prevent them as far as possible... manage... and disclose them to clients' (paras 184-200); 2.6 Client Assets - Principle 15 'adequate arrangements to safeguard the rights of clients in client assets... and, where it is reasonably possible, ensure that clients' assets are held in a Shari'ah-compliant manner' (paras 201-249); 2.7 Complaints Handling and Dispute Resolution - Principle 16 'an efficient, accessible and fair mechanism to address investor complaints... dispute resolution mechanisms that take into account Shari'ah-related issues' (paras 250-265); 2.8 Investor Education - Principle 17 'Regulators should play an active role in promoting the education and understanding of investors and other market participants in relation to the Islamic capital markets' (paras 266-281). Definitions (ICIS, Shari'ah Adviser, Sukuk). Annex: Taxonomy of Crypto-Assets (four categories). Appendix: Gap Analysis and the IFSB's Approach.
key_points: Investor protection here covers protection against misconduct by intermediaries, misleading claims of Shari'ah compliance and misuse of clients' assets; enhancing transparency; protection of minority shareholders; and effective redress or dispute resolution (para 1)

The ICM consists of three principal product markets - Islamic equities, sukuk, and ICIS; short selling and derivatives are not a feature of the ICM for Shari'ah reasons and are not addressed by the standard (para 5)

Crypto-asset provisions apply only to security tokens (fourth category of the Annex taxonomy) conferring ownership rights with a right to future profits, dividends or residual interest, where approved by relevant Shari'ah boards; other categories are the subject of Shari'ah debate (paras 9-10)
Recommended implementation is effective from January 2023 onwards, with RSAs encouraged to implement earlier where able (para 17)

Shari'ah elements of conduct: a moral screen prohibiting contracts based on substantial ignorance and uncertainty (gharar) and immoral sectors (alcohol, pornography, casinos, pork); prohibition of riba, defined as increase in return for deferment in a qard contract (riba al-nasi'ah) or exchange contract (riba al-fadl); and sanctity of contracts (para 23)

Shari'ah governance requires ex-ante and ex-post compliance monitoring: daily-operations compliance, Shari'ah approval/screening of products, periodic reviews, and purification of tainted income, with channelling to charity supervised by a Shari'ah board/adviser and disclosed (para 28, fn 9)

Best-practice Shari'ah governance includes an independent Shari'ah board/adviser issuing fatawa, BOD responsibility for appointment, a designated Shari'ah compliance function/officer, an internal Shari'ah audit, and (size-dependent) an external Shari'ah audit whose reports are shared with the public; small firms may outsource to shared centralised services or a single adviser (para 33, fn 11)
Firms carrying out both Islamic and conventional capital market activities should segregate them, e.g. via dedicated staff or unit depending on size (para 33(xv), para 5)
High-speed algorithmic trading may contravene the Shari'ah principle that a person should not sell securities he does not possess, where possession implies settlement by delivery (para 40)

Retail clients get the highest degree of investor protection; non-retail investors may elect retail categorisation if they have limited knowledge of Shari'ah-compliant instruments; opting up requires a qualitative assessment, a clear written warning of lost protections, and a client statement in a document separate from the contract (paras 44, 48, 50)

Product governance (Principle 4) requires Shari'ah and product approval processes and identified target markets; it applies to retail and professional/sophisticated clients but not market counterparties; products should be reviewed at least annually for target-market fit and continued Shari'ah compliance (paras 52-55, 63)

Regulators may impose temporary product intervention (prohibiting/restricting marketing, distribution or sale) where a product claimed as Shari'ah-compliant raises significant investor protection or Shari'ah non-compliance concerns, on a precautionary basis before marketing, and may make measures permanent if concerns are unaddressed (paras 64-66)

Where equities are officially classified as Shari'ah-compliant there must be adequate disclosure of the qualitative and quantitative screening methodology in retail-friendly language, periodic re-screening, timely disclosure of status changes, and exclusion from the compliant list if adequate issuer information ceases to be available (paras 79-82, 85)

Information on all costs and charges must be aggregated and provided at minimum annually during the life of the investment; inducements must be separately disclosed annually; portfolio-management reporting should be at least quarterly and indicate the portfolio's Shari'ah compliance (paras 90, 93, 97)

Client money held in conventional accounts (only where Shari'ah-compliant options are unavailable) requires disclosure of reasons and client consent, and any accrued interest must be distributed to charity under Shari'ah board/adviser supervision with disclosed basis and recipient bodies (para 98, para 205)

Robo-advisers must disclose the exact degree of human involvement, the mechanisms ensuring advice stays within Shari'ah compliance parameters, and information sources used; firms must monitor and test algorithms so Shari'ah non-compliant instruments are not offered to clients with a strict Shari'ah preference, with Shari'ah board/adviser oversight of inputs and outputs (paras 103, 118)

Suitability assessment must obtain the client's knowledge/experience, financial situation including ability to bear losses, and investment objectives including risk tolerance and preference for Shari'ah-compliant investments; e.g. tolerance for non-capital-guaranteed musharakah/mudarabah-based instruments versus capital-guaranteed murabahah-based instruments may need assessment (paras 108, 115)

Execution-only services in non-complex Shari'ah-compliant instruments at the client's initiative are exempt from appropriateness assessment subject to conditions; robo-adviser investment advice should not be considered a Shari'ah resolution/fatwa (paras 121-122)

Fit and proper: the BOD collectively should have knowledge and experience of Islamic finance; honesty/integrity factors include convictions for dishonesty, fraud, money laundering, theft or financial crime within the past 10 years; staff development must be reviewed at least annually with training before new Shari'ah-compliant products are offered (paras 155, 160, 153)

Best execution may factor in availability of a dedicated Islamic securities exchange platform and Shari'ah-compliant trade/post-trade services; Shari'ah-compliant margin financing is a qard provided without any monetary or non-monetary excess on the principal, impermissible if it includes hidden interest; firms must publish execution-quality reports at least annually (paras 167, 170, fn 23)

Conflicts of interest: independent advice must assess a sufficiently diverse range of instruments not limited to closely linked entities; firms must not accept and retain third-party fees/commissions for independent advice or portfolio management except minor non-monetary benefits meeting four conditions; disclosure of conflicts is a measure of last resort (paras 191-193, 196)

Client assets: separately titled accounts, reconciliations consistent with account activity and daily against a central securities depository, records specifying each client's rights daily and whether assets are held in a Shari'ah-compliant manner; a qualifying Shari'ah-compliant money market fund must aim to maintain at least the investors' initial capital and provide same-day or next-day redemption (paras 201-202, 209, 221-222, fn 27)

In firm-failure measures such as client and settlement takaful schemes or third-party guarantee funds, providing third-party guarantee funds in return for a fee is not Shari'ah-compliant unless it is based on actual and direct cost; liens/rights of set-off over client assets for unrelated debts are not permitted except where required by foreign law, with Shari'ah principles taken into consideration (para 219, fn 25, para 227)

Complaints and redress mechanisms (including ombudsman/ADR) must take account of Shari'ah-related issues, be accessible by electronic means without physical presence, and be free of charge; Shari'ah-related complaints should interact with the firm's Shari'ah governance bodies up to its Shari'ah board; regulators should promote investor education covering screening methodologies and purification, without giving specific investment advice (paras 251, 256-257, 268, 273)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: providing third-party guarantee funds in return for a fee is not Shari'ah-compliant unless it is based on actual and direct cost (fn 25, attached to para 219 on client/settlement takaful schemes or guarantee funds established by a third party)
clauses: Bearing in mind that providing third-party guarantee funds in return for a fee is not Shari'ah-compliant unless it is based on actual and direct cost. (fn 25)

applying available measures intended to minimise client, counterparty and systemic risk in the event of a firm's failure, such as client and settlement takaful schemes or guarantee funds established by a third party (para 219(iii))

divergence_notes: Crypto-assets treated as currencies: 'This category of crypto-assets is the subject of Shari'ah debate and is not addressed in this standard' (para 9)

Crypto-asset categories other than security tokens 'are not within the scope of this standard and are the subject of Shari'ah debate' (para 10); Annex likewise states there is less consensus on non-security-token crypto-assets and 'they are the subject of Shari'ah debate' (Annex)

Dispute resolution anticipates conflicting Shari'ah interpretations: where a complaint is unsettled 'because the firm or investor insists on a particular Shari'ah interpretation, the external institution for dispute resolution should be able to understand whether the Shari'ah stance of the firm/investor is well-founded' (para 263)

Screening methodologies differ across jurisdictions: firms marketing foreign products must disclose the screening methodology and issuing authority where the compliance claim relies on a foreign centralised Shari'ah board's criteria, or the basis of the claim where the foreign jurisdiction has no centralised Shari'ah governance system (paras 37-38)

standards.applicability: Requirements to be applied by regulatory and supervisory authorities (RSAs) to takāful undertakings (TUs) and retakāful undertakings (RTUs) (para 4), whether operating under general, family or composite licences, though some disclosures are specific to family TUs/RTUs; RSAs may choose not to apply all participant disclosures to RTUs because retakāful is a business transaction between professional entities (para 11). Developed around the hybrid model adopted by most TUs/RTUs but applicable with appropriate modifications to other models, e.g. the mutual model used in Sudan and the cooperative model used in Saudi Arabia (para 9). Primary focus is disclosures at the legal entity (solo) level, with references to group disclosures at certain points (para 10). Also addresses takāful/retakāful windows, which are not separate legal entities (paras 11, 184-188), and microtakāful (paras 189-191). Proportionality applies by nature, scale and complexity — it may not be appropriate to apply all requirements to very small TUs/RTUs (para 13); the supervisor may decide not to apply prudential disclosure requirements at all in exceptional situations, e.g. captive TOs (para 21). The standard does not deal with supervisory reporting, i.e. information provided only to the RSA (para 7).
standards.structure: Section 1: Introduction — 1.1 Background; 1.2 Objectives; 1.3 Scope, Approach and Application; 1.4 Implementation Date (paras 1-15). Section 2: Disclosures for Takāful/Retakāful Undertakings — 2.1 Prudential Disclosures (paras 16-127) with subsections 2.1.1 Company profile; 2.1.2 Corporate governance; 2.1.3 Sharīʻah governance; 2.1.4 Technical provisions; 2.1.5 Takāful risk exposure; 2.1.6 Financial instruments and other investments; 2.1.7 Investment risk exposures; 2.1.8 Asset–liability management; 2.1.9 Capital adequacy; 2.1.10 Liquidity risk; 2.1.11 Financial performance; 2.2 Conduct of Business Disclosures (paras 128-179) with 2.2.1 Distribution of takāful products, 2.2.2 Prior to inception of the contract, 2.2.3 After inception of the contract; 2.3 Environmental, Social, Governance (ESG) Disclosures (paras 180-181). Section 3: Additional Specific Issues — 3.1 Retakāful (paras 182-183); 3.2 Takāful/Retakāful Windows (paras 184-188); 3.3 Microtakāful (paras 189-191). Definitions. Appendix: Mapping of the IAIS ICPs and the IFSB Approach (ICP 20 standards 20.3-20.13 amended/deleted; ICP 19 conduct standards amended; additional new standards on Sharīʻah governance, ESG, and retakāful/windows/microtakāful). Requirements are framed as boxed supervisory standards followed by numbered guidance paragraphs 1-191.
key_points: Standard responds to a recommendation of the 2005 IFSB-IAIS Joint Working Group paper 'Issues in Regulation and Supervision of Takāful (Islamic Insurance)'; the JWG identified four themes: corporate governance, financial and prudential regulation, transparency/reporting/market conduct, and the supervisory review process (paras 1-2)

Covers two types of disclosure — public prudential disclosures for market discipline (analogous to Basel Pillar 3 and EU Solvency II) and disclosures to participants and potential participants; it does not deal with supervisory reporting (para 7, fn 3)

Takāful specificities requiring disclosure beyond conventional insurance include multiple funds within a single legal entity with financial flows between them, Sharīʻah governance including a Sharīʻah-compliant investment programme, and possible surplus distributions to participants (para 5)
Built around the hybrid takāful model; applicable with appropriate modifications to the mutual model used in Sudan and the cooperative model used in Saudi Arabia (para 9)

RSAs may choose not to apply participant disclosures to RTUs because retakāful is a business transaction between professional entities; RSAs commonly impose limited, if any, customer disclosure requirements in retakāful/reinsurance transactions (paras 11, 182)
Recommended implementation by RSAs effective from January 2023 onwards, with an adequate pre-implementation period from the issuance date; earlier implementation encouraged (para 14)

Supervisor may decide not to apply prudential disclosure requirements at all where there is no threat to the financial system, no public interest need and no legitimately interested party prevented from information — expected to be exceptional, e.g. captive TOs (para 21)

TOs/RTOs make audited financial statements available at least annually, and disclose at least annually appropriately detailed information on 11 areas: company profile, corporate governance, Sharīʻah governance, technical provisions, takāful risk exposure, financial instruments and other investments, investment risk exposures, asset–liability management, capital adequacy, liquidity risk, and financial performance (paras 30-31)

Company profile must summarise the operating model used (wakālah, muḍārabah, waqf, hybrid models, etc.), including the contracts used, the structure of funds within the TU/RTU, and actual or potential flows of money between them (para 38)

Segregation of the shareholders' fund and participants' funds (PRF and PIF) must be maintained at all times as a fiduciary responsibility; TOs/RTOs should disclose how they maintain segregation and manage conflicts of interest between shareholders and participants (para 46)

Sharīʻah governance disclosures cover 13 specified items including board responsibility statement, Sharīʻah board members' names, qualifications, meeting attendance and remuneration, fatāwā with supporting basis, departures from previous fatāwā with reasoning, Sharīʻah non-compliance events with the amount of Sharīʻah non-compliant income and the rectification process, and non-financial non-compliance events with control measures (para 49)

For each fund, TOs/RTOs disclose the adopted Sharīʻah screening methodology, purification payments made for assets or business not fully Sharīʻah-compliant, and the amount of purification payments held and not yet paid (para 51)

Where TOs/RTOs pay zakat on behalf of shareholders or participants they disclose the calculation method, amount paid each year, recipient institutions and amount held unpaid; if the TO/RTO does not pay zakat, sufficient information must be disclosed to allow stakeholders to calculate their own zakat contributions (paras 52-53)

Technical provisions are disclosed for each PRF, presented gross of retakāful/reinsurance (net also useful), and may be presented in two parts: claims provisions for events already occurred (including IBNR and IBNER) and provisions for future events (sum of provision for unearned contributions and provision for unexpired risks, also termed 'contribution deficiency reserve') (paras 54-55, 62)

Except for short-tail business, the supervisor may require general TOs to disclose claims development triangles, reported consistently on an accident year or underwriting year basis and reconciled to the balance sheet; general TOs disclose mean cost of claims incurred and claims frequency by class, separately for each PRF (paras 69, 120)

Where a TU/RTU makes material use of conventional, rather than takāful, reinsurance/retrocession it should explain for each line of business why this has been done; reliance of TOs/RTOs on conventional reinsurance is based on the concept of need (ḥājah) (para 75, fn 15)

Disclosures cover use of Sharīʻah-compliant hedging mechanisms (not conventional derivatives) for takāful and investment risks, with reference to OIC Fiqh Academy Resolution no. 238 (9/24) and AAOIFI Sharīʻah standard no. 45; the IAIS derivatives paragraph was deleted in the ICP mapping (paras 73, 90, 96, fn 14)

Investment risk exposures (currency risk, market risk, credit risk in operational activities, concentration risk) are disclosed both in aggregate and fund-by-fund, since correlation of risk among PRF, PIF and SHF may affect the SHF's ability to support the PRF, and the PIF's ability to contribute to the PRF (paras 84-85)
Stress-testing disclosure example: the change in capital resources as a percentage of total assets corresponding to a 100-basis point change in profit rates (para 91)

Capital adequacy is disclosed separately for SHF and PRF against regulatory requirements (minimum capital requirement and prescribed capital requirement for PRFs; minimum target capital and prescribed target capital for SHF); TOs/RTOs must disclose resources available in the SHF to provide qarḍ or other support to the PRF, and whether any PRF capital resources are available for distribution to participants and under what conditions (paras 99, 101-102)

Financial performance disclosures include transfers between funds and the sources of SHF income including wakālah fees and muḍārib's share, plus how common income and expenses are allocated between funds; general TOs disclose claims, expense, combined and operating ratios calculated gross of retakāful/reinsurance on an accident year or underwriting year basis, with both gross and net ratios if materially different; discount rates disclosed by duration for each of the next five years and the average rate for claims expected to be paid after five years (paras 111-112, 115-117)

Pre-contract disclosures for investment-based takāful include the profit-sharing ratio where a muḍārabah contract is used to manage investments, the frequency of investment profit and/or underwriting surplus declaration, whether performance figures are actual, simulated or forecast, comparison of actual PIF return with benchmark over RSA-defined timescales, and the identity and remuneration of the fund manager; for each PIF the TO describes investment objective, strategy, strategic asset allocation and performance benchmark (paras 148-149)

ESG disclosures are modelled on the FSB's Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures across four areas: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets (para 181, fn 33); during economic stress (e.g. COVID-19 contribution deferrals) TOs must communicate clearly about Sharīʻah-compliant relief offered and disclose PIF performance more frequently at times of high market volatility (paras 171-172, fn 31)

Takāful/retakāful windows should be required to disclose as though free-standing TUs/RTUs, plus their organisational relationship with the conventional host, arrangements for segregation of funds from the host, possible flows of funds between window and host (e.g. profit-sharing portion and wakālah fee), joint transactions such as joint retakāful/reinsurance placement, and any support from the host (e.g. qarḍ without interest) given in the past and not yet repaid (paras 185-188); microtakāful (based on tabarruʻ, taʻawun and prohibition of ribā) requires proportionality and simplified product literature understandable by a low-income population (paras 189-191, fn 37)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: acknowledges tawarruq as a liquidity tool — the SHF may enter 'into a tawarruq arrangement to obtain liquidity, in which case the financer is considered a creditor of the SHF' (fn 5); no divergence discussion in this standard

IFSB: 'There are Shari'ah issues around the use of derivatives as normally understood', so the guidance refers instead to the use of Sharīʻah-compliant hedging mechanisms, citing OIC Fiqh Academy Resolution no. 238 (9/24) and AAOIFI Sharīʻah standard no. 45; the IAIS ICP 20.7 paragraph on derivatives was deleted (Appendix mapping, ICP 20.7 row; paras 73, 90; fn 14)

divergence_notes: Conventional reinsurance accommodation: 'the reliance of TOs/RTOs on conventional reinsurance is based on the concept of need (ḥājah)' (fn 15); where material use is made of conventional reinsurance/retrocession, the TU/RTU 'should explain for each line of business why this has been done' (para 75)

Takāful models vary by jurisdiction: the standard is built on the hybrid model but notes 'the mutual model used in Sudan and the cooperative model used in Saudi Arabia', applicable 'with appropriate modifications' (para 9)

Compulsory takāful bundled with goods/services is Sharīʻah-unsettled: 'The Sharīʻah compliance of such practice needs to be reviewed by the Sharīʻah board on a case-by-case basis, especially where it is compulsory for the client to obtain takāful' (fn 26)

Sharīʻah board positions may change: disclosure required of 'any departures by the Shari'ah board from its previous fatāwā, or revisions to those fatāwā, and the reasoning for such departure or revision' (para 49(viii))

key_points: An FMI is defined as a multilateral system among participating institutions, including the operator, used for clearing, settling, or recording payments, securities, or other financial transactions, and covers five key types: payment systems, CSDs, SSSs, CCPs and TRs (paras 9-10).

The standard complements the CPSS-IOSCO PFMI (April 2012) and its Disclosure Framework and Assessment Methodology (December 2012), following a 'comprehensive' approach that retains unamended conventional principles and adds a new Principle 25 on Sharīʻah governance plus Islamic-specific material at the Key Consideration, Question and Explanatory Note levels (paras 6, 19-20).
Recommended implementation date is from January 2024 onwards, with an adequate pre-implementation period from the standard's issuance date; RSAs are encouraged to implement earlier if able (para 27).

Sharīʻah non-compliance risk (SNCR) is defined per the IFSB Glossary as 'an operational risk resulting from non-compliance of the institution with the rules and principles of Sharīʻah in its products and services,' managed via Sharīʻah governance arrangements under Principle 25 (para 30).

Derivatives and short selling are, for Sharīʻah reasons, not material features of the Islamic capital market (ICM), mitigating some conventional FMI risks, though this also means fewer conventional hedging instruments are available to Islamic FMIs (para 29).
'Hedging' by Islamic FMIs is limited to the types of hedging defined in International Fiqh Academy Resolution No. 238 (24/9), issued 6 November 2019 (para 29).

CCPs face the greatest SNCR issues among FMI types because they hold substantial financial resources/collateral and operate default (guarantee) funds; a CCP is characterised, from a Sharīʻah perspective, as undertaking settlement of transactions by delivery of assets and payments and is not treated as a buyer or seller of the transaction's origin (para 34, fn 13).

Footnotes to Principle 4 state that a CCP's default/guarantee fund is 'not generally based on a guarantee contract as such contracts are normally understood' and that treating the CCP's settlement role this way 'does not imply a contract of guarantee (kafalah)' (fn 12, fn 13).

Principle 4 (Credit risk): a CCP must establish initial collateral requirements meeting an established single-tailed confidence level of at least 99 percent of the estimated distribution of future exposure, applied at the portfolio or more-granular level as relevant (para 114).

Principle 4: any financial/late-payment penalty fee imposed for delay is to be channelled to charity on the basis of a prior commitment, after deducting the FMI's actual direct costs incurred (fn 28, paras 111-113).

Principle 6 (Calculation of collateral): a CCP's collateral system must be Sharīʻah-compliant as approved by its Sharīʻah board; where a CCP operates a dual (Islamic/conventional) system it must ensure separation between the Sharīʻah-compliant and non-compliant collateral systems (paras 137-138).

Principle 9 (Money settlements): an FMI should neither receive nor pay interest on the accounts used for money settlements; if interest receipt is unavoidable, it must be treated as non-Sharīʻah-compliant income and channelled to charity as approved by the Sharīʻah board (Key Consideration 6, para 196).

Principle 14 (Segregation and portability): where a CCP operates a dual system, it should establish separate omnibus accounts for Islamic and conventional businesses to avoid commingling of collateral (para 234).

Principle 15 (General business risk): an FMI must hold liquid net assets funded by equity equal to at least six months of current operating expenses (excluding depreciation/amortisation), in addition to resources held for participant defaults or other financial-resource risks (para 247, fn 123).

Principle 16 (Custody and investment risks): an FMI's investment strategy must be consistent with Sharīʻah requirements, distinguished clearly where the FMI operates a dual system, secured by or claims on high-quality obligors, and must allow for quick liquidation with little adverse price effect (para 257).

Principle 17 (Operational risk): an FMI's business continuity plan should be designed to enable critical IT systems to resume operations within two hours following disruptive events and to enable completion of settlement by the end of the day even in extreme circumstances (para 272).

Principle 21 (Efficiency and effectiveness): a TR should ideally record transaction information from participants to its central registry in real time and, at a minimum, within one business day (para 330).

Principle 23 (Disclosure): an FMI should complete and disclose responses to the disclosure framework for Islamic FMIs regularly and, at a minimum, review these responses for accuracy every two years (para 346).

Principle 25 (Sharīʻah governance) is a wholly new principle with no CPSS-IOSCO equivalent, requiring FMIs claiming Sharīʻah compliance to have a sound Sharīʻah governance framework, including a Sharīʻah board comprising, per IFSB-10, three or more Sharīʻah scholars, a Sharīʻah advisory firm or an individual scholar, proportionate to the FMI's size and complexity (para 357).

Principle 25 requires internal Sharīʻah compliance review/audit plus an annual (external) Sharīʻah compliance review/audit, procedures for issuing and disseminating Sharīʻah pronouncements, and procedures for obtaining emergency Sharīʻah rulings/fatwās during unforeseen events such as a crisis (Key Considerations 5 and 7, paras 355-364).

Islamic repurchase agreements arranged by an FMI should follow the relevant AAOIFI Sharīʻah standard on repurchase agreements, or otherwise fulfil Sharīʻah requirements stipulated by the relevant jurisdiction's Sharīʻah boards where the AAOIFI standard is not implemented (fn 151, para 340).

Where collateral changes status from Sharīʻah-compliant to non-Sharīʻah-compliant during the FMI's holding period, the FMI should seek a replacement from the participant where applicable; the Sharīʻah ruling is that collateral remains in the ownership of the pledgor (paras 125, 134).

An 'affiliate' for credit-exposure aggregation purposes is defined as a company that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with a participant, with control defined as ownership/voting power of 20 percent or more of a class of voting securities, or consolidation for financial reporting purposes (fn 32).

Responsibility D requires authorities to adopt the IFSB CPIFRFMI and apply the principles, at a minimum, to all systemically important payment systems, CSDs, SSSs, CCPs and TRs, consistently within and across jurisdictions (paras 376-378).

fn 13: 'does not imply a contract of guarantee (kafalah)... The fundamental function of a CCP is to place itself between the buyer and seller of an original trade and effectively guarantee the obligations under the contract agreed between the two parties...'

divergence_notes: "An FMI conducting business in multiple jurisdictions should identify and mitigate the risks arising from any potential conflict of laws or Sharīʿah interpretations across jurisdictions" (Principle 1, Key Consideration 5; para 61).

"Where an FMI conducts its business in multiple jurisdictions, it should assess and manage the risk that different Sharīʿah interpretations may have implications for the legal basis on which it operates" (para 61).
"An FMI that establishes a link is exposed to possible Sharīʿah risk that may result from different Sharīʻah interpretations (e.g. cross-collateral between CCPs)" (fn 141, para 306).

"Different interpretations of Sharīʿah have always posed a hindrance to cross-border activities within the ICM... even where harmonisation cannot be achieved, understanding of relevant differences may be important in assessing the risks posed to FMIs in cross-border operations" (para 381).

Responsibility E, Key Consideration 11: relevant authorities should promote Sharīʻah harmonisation with jurisdictions where their FMIs have cooperation arrangements, and where this is not achievable, should understand the differences in interpretation important to assessing risks posed to FMIs (Responsibility E, Key Consideration 11).

standards.applicability: Applies to takāful, with 'takāful' including retakāful unless otherwise stated (para 13); addressed to regulatory and supervisory authorities (RSAs) of the takāful sector, and applies to the supervision of takāful undertakings (TU = the takāful operator together with the funds it manages) and, unless otherwise specified, to insurance groups, the head of the insurance group, and takāful operations within insurance groups (para 16); also applies to takāful windows of conventional insurers (para 18; TCP 26) and to takāful intermediaries (TCP 18). Developed primarily by reference to the 'hybrid' takāful structure, but provisions apply, where relevant and with modification, to other models of takāful or Islamic insurance (paras 30-31). Where a supervisor covers both conventional insurance and takāful, the standard applies separately in respect of its supervision of takāful (para 32). TCPs are minimum requirements to be applied proportionately to nature, scale and complexity (paras 33-34). TCP 22 (AML/CFT) applies to underwriting and placement of family takāful and other investment-related takāful, with jurisdictional discretion whether to extend it to general takāful (para 22.0.8). Section 2: Takāful Core Principles, comprising 26 TCPs (24 IAIS ICPs adapted plus 2 new principles, para 24): TCP 1: Objectives, Powers and Responsibilities of the Supervisor; TCP 2: Supervisor; TCP 3: Information Sharing and Confidentiality Requirements; TCP 4: Licensing; TCP 5: Suitability of Persons; TCP 6: Change of Control and Portfolio Transfers; TCP 7: Corporate Governance; TCP 8: Sharī`ah Governance (new, no IAIS ICP equivalent); TCP 9: Risk Management and Internal Controls; TCP 10: Supervisory Review and Reporting; TCP 11: Preventive Measures, Corrective Measures and Sanctions; TCP 12: Exit from the Market and Resolution; TCP 13: Retakāful and Other Forms of Risk Sharing; TCP 14: Valuation; TCP 15: Investments; TCP 16: Enterprise Risk Management for Solvency Purposes; TCP 17: Capital Adequacy; TCP 18: Intermediaries; TCP 19: Conduct of Business; TCP 20: Public Disclosure; TCP 21: Countering Fraud in Takāful; TCP 22: Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism; TCP 23: Group-Wide Supervision; TCP 24: Macroprudential Supervision; TCP 25: Supervisory Cooperation and Coordination; TCP 26: Window Operations (new, no IAIS ICP equivalent). key_points: Standard sets out takāful core principles (TCPs) closely aligned with the IAIS ICPs as adopted in November 2019, modifying and adding to them as necessary to reflect the application of Sharī'ah principles in takāful (para 8)

Built on the 24 IAIS ICPs (the ICPs are numbered 1 to 25 but there is no longer a separate ICP 11); two further principles are added — Sharī'ah governance (TCP 8) and window operation (TCP 26) — giving 26 TCPs, with a correspondence table in Appendix 2 (paras 22, 24, fn 9)

TCP material hierarchy: principle statements, standards (which should be met to demonstrate observance) and guidance (which does not represent requirements); assessment methodology grades each standard and principle statement as observed, largely observed, partly observed, not observed, or not applicable (paras 25, 62-63)
Recommended observance date: RSAs should observe the standard effective from July 2024 onwards, taking into account an adequate preparatory period from issuance; earlier adoption encouraged (para 48)

Specificities of takāful include the tabarru' commitment, ta'awun (mutual assistance) whereby speculative risk (maisir) is avoided and uncertainty (ghārar) mitigated, segregated funds — one SHF plus one or more risk-bearing takāful funds (PRFs bearing insurance risk and PIFs bearing investment risk) — and a commitment to Shari'ah compliance in all activities (para 19, fn 5)

Fund deficits may be covered by retained surpluses or by a qarḍ (qarḍ hasan — a loan without remuneration, repaying only principal) provided from the SHF or a third party, repaid out of future surpluses; where a deficit is due to the TO's negligence or misconduct, the operator must compensate the takāful fund (para 19, fn 7, fn 8)

The opinion of the IFSB Shari'ah board is that the SHF should not receive any surplus of a takāful fund, based on the resolution of the International Fiqh Academy, though investment income may be attributed in part to the SHF as mudarib's share (fn 6)

Reference to takāful includes retakāful; the standard is developed primarily by reference to the hybrid takāful structure (a two-tier mutual/commercial hybrid per IFSB-8 para 5) but applies with modification to other models (paras 13, 29-31, fn 10)

Licensing: business and financial plans must be projected for a minimum of three years; conventional insurers seeking a takāful window licence must demonstrate systems managing window risks separately from the host; supervisors may refuse a name or advertising implying Islamic business where consumers would be misled (paras 4.3.2, 4.3.8, 4.2.2)

Change of control: supervisors typically establish lower notification thresholds (such as between 5% and 10%) for initial notification of acquiring control, with higher percentages for approval and increased control (para 6.2.2)

Sharī'ah board members must meet fit-and-proper requirements; IFSB-10 states a Sharī'ah board should have at least three members; approvals based on dharura (necessity) should be time-limited and revisited at the end of that time or earlier if circumstances change (paras 8.2.2, 8.3.3, fn 12)

Risk management systems must cover at least underwriting and reserving, asset-liability management, investments, liquidity, concentration, Sharī'ah non-compliance, operational and conduct risks; Sharī'ah non-compliance risk is classified as a form of operational risk; ORSA must consider the risk that relevant fatāwā change or understanding of Sharī'ah develops; continuity analysis should use a horizon of e.g. 3 to 5 years (paras 9.1.3, 16.1.2, 16.12.3, 16.14.7)

Supervisory reporting must include presentation at the level of each segregated fund, including assets, liabilities, technical balances, solvency position, and qarḍ used or available for use (para 10.4.4)

Supervisory powers include fund-level directions: restricting attribution of income/expense items, prohibiting acceptance of new business into a fund, restricting or prohibiting repayment of subordinated qarḍ, requiring surplus retention within a fund, restricting transfer of wakālah fee and investment income from a PRF or PIF to the SHF, and facilitating transfer of fund management to another TO (para 11.2.7)

Resolution: within a takāful fund losses are absorbed in the order (i) all capital resources recognised for solvency purposes, (ii) creditors subordinated by agreement to takāful participants, (iii) takāful participants' entitlements; the NCWOL (no creditor worse off than in liquidation) principle applies; continuity of some general takāful contracts may be needed only for a short period (e.g., 30 or 60 days) (paras 12.0.11, 12.2.2, 12.0.8)

The IFSB Shari'ah Board is of the view that the creditor hierarchy from the Shari'ah perspective places qarḍ ahead of takāful participant claims, except where the creditor has explicitly agreed to subordination of the qarḍ (fn 15)

Retakāful: a TO's use of conventional reinsurance — often defended by reference to dharurah (necessity) — must be subject to appropriate Sharī'ah governance; dharurah decisions must specify a review term or trigger conditions and be reviewed at least annually; cash flows under retakāful contracts must be attributed fairly between funds with a documented policy (paras 13.1.1-13.1.4, 13.4.3-13.4.4)

Valuation for solvency purposes uses a total balance sheet approach on an economic basis; technical provisions comprise a current estimate plus a margin over the current estimate (MOCE), valued separately for each fund including the SHF, and must not reflect the TU's own credit standing; contract boundaries defined by three constraints (contractual termination/unilateral options, TO's unilateral cancellation right, bilateral continuation decisions) (paras 14.0.4-14.0.6, 14.6.1, 14.7.1, 14.7.4, 14.8.4)

Investments must be undertaken on a Sharī'ah-compliant basis; income tainted by impermissible activities may require forfeiture by way of purification; there are Sharī'ah issues around derivatives as normally understood, so guidance refers to hedging mechanisms which can be Sharī'ah-compliant, citing OIC Fiqh Academy Resolution no. 238 (9/24) and AAOIFI Sharī'ah standard no. 45; diversification and other qualitative requirements apply at the level of the segregated fund (paras 15.0.2, 15.0.4, 15.2.3-15.2.4, fn 21)

Capital adequacy is assessed at the level of each segregated fund, with a supervisory presumption that capital resources within segregated funds are not fungible between funds unless the contrary is demonstrated; solvency control levels (PCR — above which no capital-grounds intervention; MCR — triggering strongest actions, with a minimum viability bound) apply at each fund including the SHF; the PCR/MCR of the TU as a whole may be the sum of its constituent funds' PCRs/MCRs where funds are non-fungible (paras 17.1.1, 17.1.3, 17.5, 17.5.1, 17.5.15)

Qarḍ paid in, or an irrevocable earmarked qarḍ facility committed from the SHF, may be recognised as capital resources of a takāful fund only if capable of absorbing losses and subordinated (achievable by voluntary and irrevocable agreement of the provider); to avoid double counting and internal leverage the amounts must be excluded or deducted from SHF capital resources (or added to the SHF's PCR and MCR); repayment or release should be restricted where the fund would foreseeably fail its PCR (paras 17.11.11-17.11.15, 17.11.19-17.11.20, 17.12.14, 17.12.29)

Target criteria examples for regulatory capital calibration include a 99.5% VaR confidence level over one year, a 99% TVaR over one year, and a 95% TVaR over the term of the takāful contract obligations; an example tiering approach sets a minimum level of 50% of required capital in high-quality elements and an upper limit of 25% for lowest-quality capital (paras 17.9.3, 17.13.10, 17.12.46)

Public disclosure: TOs must disclose at least annually their Sharī'ah governance framework including Sharī'ah board membership, qualifications, remuneration and fatāwā, Sharī'ah non-compliance events with and without financial implications and their rectification, purification payments made and held, zakat calculation method and amounts, and the financial position of each segregated fund including qarḍ advanced (paras 20.2, 20.5.2, 20.5.4-20.5.6, 19.14.6)

Window operations (TCP 26): supervisors apply to windows requirements no more favourable than those applicable to TUs with head office in the same jurisdiction; window operation requires prior supervisory approval, effective segregation of window funds from the host (funds attributable to takāful participants are not transferred to the host), corporate and Sharī'ah governance comparable to a full-fledged TU, and capital adequacy applied at the level of the window (TCP 26; paras 26.2, 26.3.1-26.3.2, 26.4.1, 26.5.1, 26.6.3)

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: 'There are Sharī`ah issues around the use of derivatives as normally understood', so the guidance refers to hedging mechanisms 'which can be Sharīʻah-compliant' (referring for detailed analysis to OIC Fiqh Academy Resolution no. 238 (9/24) and AAOIFI Sharīʻah standard no. 45); if a TU is permitted, following due Sharīʻah governance, to make use of derivatives for risk management purposes, the unmodified guidance of ICP 15 is followed for those instruments; hedging arrangements should preferably be used for risk management rather than speculation

divergence_notes: 'The opinion of the IFSB Shari'ah board is, from the Shari'ah perspective, that the SHF should not receive any surplus of a takaful fund. This opinion is based on the resolution of the International Fiqh Academy.' (fn 6)

(para 8.0.2, fn 11)

'The cession of risks to conventional reinsurers is often defended by reference to the precept of dharurah (necessity)'; the supervisor may not have authority or capability to form an opinion on whether the conditions for dharurah are met (paras 13.1.2-13.1.3)

standards.applicability: Applicable to supervision of takāful undertakings (TUs) and retakāful undertakings (RTUs), whether operating under a general, family or composite licence, and, mutatis mutandis, to takāful 'window' operations where such operations exist (para 12). Expressed in terms of a typical two-tier hybrid TU model (mutual + proprietary with segregated funds) but applicable to other models of Islamic insurance with appropriate modifications (para 11). Focuses on the TU as a single undertaking, with section 3.7 guidance on group-wide supervision where a TU or takāful holding company heads a group; it does not apply directly to non-takāful entities within a group, but applies to TUs regarding risks posed to them by non-takāful entities (para 13). RSAs should apply proportionality by nature, scale and complexity, e.g. modified application for microtakāful providers (para 14).
standards.structure: Section 1: Introduction — 1.1 Background, 1.2 Objectives, 1.3 Specificities of Takāful, 1.4 Scope/Approach/Application, 1.5 Structure, 1.6 Effective Date (paras 1-18). Section 2: Valuation (core principle: supervisor establishes valuation requirements for solvency purposes), containing Standard I 'The valuation addresses recognition, derecognition and measurement of assets and liabilities' (para 28); Standard II 'The valuation of assets and liabilities is undertaken on consistent bases' (para 34); Standard III 'The valuation of assets and liabilities is undertaken in a reliable, decision-useful and transparent manner' (para 41); Standard IV 'The valuation of assets and liabilities is an economic valuation' (para 53); Standard V 'An economic valuation of assets and liabilities reflects the risk-adjusted present values of their cash flows' (para 55); Standard VI 'The value of technical provisions and other liabilities does not reflect the TU's own credit standing' (para 73); Standard VII 'The valuation of technical provisions exceeds the current estimate by a margin (margin over the current estimate, or MOCE)' (para 77); Standard VIII 'The current estimate reflects the expected present value of all relevant future cash flows that arise in fulfilling takāful obligations, using unbiased, current assumptions' (para 89); Standard IX 'The MOCE reflects the inherent uncertainty related to all relevant future cash flows that arise in fulfilling takāful obligations over the full-time horizon thereof' (para 106); Standard X 'The valuation of technical provisions allows for time preference. The supervisor establishes criteria for the determination of appropriate rates to be used in the discounting of technical provisions' (para 116); Standard XI 'The supervisor requires the valuation of technical provisions to make appropriate allowance for embedded options and other features' (para 122). Section 3: Regulatory Capital Requirements (core principle: supervisor establishes capital adequacy requirements so TUs can absorb significant unforeseen losses and to provide for degrees of supervisory intervention) — 3.1 Introduction (para 125); 3.2 Segregation of Funds with Standard XII 'The supervisor assesses capital adequacy at the level of the segregated fund...' (para 128); 3.3 Total Balance Sheet Approach with Standard XIII (para 134); 3.4 Establishing Regulatory Capital Requirements with Standard XIV (capital at sufficient level, para 140), Standard XV (solvency control levels trigger degrees of intervention, para 153), Standard XVI (PCR and MCR defined, para 162), Standard XVII (open, transparent process; standardised and approved tailored approaches, para 178), Standard XVIII (all relevant and material risk categories addressed and explicit allocation between technical provisions and capital requirements, para 189), Standard XIX (target criteria for calibration, para 197), Standard XX (variations to requirements in transparent framework and limited circumstances, para 218); 3.5 Identification and Assessment of Capital Resources with Standard XXI (approach to determining eligible capital resources, para 223) and Standard XXII (criteria for quality and suitability of capital resources, going concern and wind-up loss absorbency, para 258); 3.6 Use of an Internal Model with Standard XXIV (modelling criteria, prior approval, statistical quality/calibration/use tests, documentation, ongoing validation, para 319) — no heading labelled 'Standard XXIII' appears in the text between Standards XXII and XXIV; 3.7 Additional Considerations for Insurance Groups and TUs that are Members of Groups (paras 329-384). key_points: IFSB-28 revises IFSB-11 (December 2010); the IFSB Council agreed to the revision at its 35th meeting in Dhaka, Bangladesh, on 14 December 2019, and RSAs are recommended to observe the Standard from December 2024, earlier where possible (paras 1, 3, 17)

Objectives: protect takāful participants by setting a high probability that a TU will meet all contractual obligations; encourage early warning systems permitting proportionate intervention and avoiding procyclical effects; foster public confidence in the takāful sector (para 5)

Specificities of takāful include the tabarru' commitment, ta'āwun (mutual assistance, avoiding maisir and rendering ghārar acceptable), segregation of funds (SHF plus one or more risk-bearing takāful funds — PRFs bearing insurance risk and PIFs bearing investment risk), attribution of surpluses and deficits to participants collectively, and commitment to Sharī'ah compliance (para 6, fn 6)

The IFSB Sharī'ah board's opinion, based on the resolution of the International Fiqh Academy, is that the SHF should not receive any underwriting surplus of a takāful fund; investment income arising in the fund may be in part attributed to the SHF as the muḍārib share (fn 7)

Qarḍ in the Standard means qarḍ hasan — a loan without remuneration, repayable only at the principal amount advanced (fn 9); to the extent a deficit is due to the negligence or misconduct of the TO, the TO is responsible for compensating the takāful fund (para 6)

Two key possible recognition points for takāful contracts are the bound date and the inception date; ceded retakāful surpluses in the RTU's PRF are not recognised until distribution to the cedant is formally approved, and a conventional reinsurance arrangement entered in exceptional circumstances following due Sharī'ah governance does not derecognise technical provisions unless the primary contracts are extinguished or novated (paras 29, 31, 33)

Amortised cost values must be evaluated for adequacy at least annually; because of the avoidance of ribā, future cash flows on TU assets (particularly on maturity) may not be certain, so supervisors may approach amortised cost valuation with caution for takāful solvency purposes (paras 67-69, 72)

The value of technical provisions and other liabilities must not reflect the TU's own credit standing; this extends to qarḍ balances between funds — deterioration in a fund's credit standing must not reduce the qarḍ liability in the takāful fund, though it is relevant to the corresponding SHF asset (paras 73, 75)

Technical provisions comprise the current estimate (probability-weighted expected present value of all relevant cash flows) plus a MOCE covering inherent uncertainty; the MOCE sits in the segregated fund responsible for the obligations and, because capital is not fungible between funds, determining current estimate and MOCE at fund level may produce higher technical provisions than a TU-wide determination (paras 77, 82-83, 85)

Contract boundary constraints for the current estimate: contractual termination as extended by any unilateral participant option; the TO having a unilateral right to cancel or freely re-underwrite; or bilateral decisions on continuation — most general takāful contracts are written for only one year and cash flows beyond the TO's unilateral cancellation point are excluded (paras 92-94)

Distributions of surplus to takāful participants and calls for additional contributions are capital flows, not takāful contract cash flows, and are brought to account only when foreseeable; accumulated surplus (including inherited surplus) that can absorb losses is a core element of a takāful fund's capital resources, ranking after creditors and takāful contract entitlements in winding-up (paras 78, 89, 98, 260)

Foreseeable payments and any amount to be paid out in purification of income determined to be tainted must be excluded from capital resources (recognised as a liability or deducted); assets or income requiring purification are excluded from capital resources (paras 98, 251)

Capital adequacy is assessed at the level of each segregated fund, including the SHF; supervisors should operate from a presumption that capital resources within segregated funds are not fungible between funds unless the contrary can be demonstrated, and no credit should be taken for diversification between non-fungible funds (paras 128, 130, 191)

No takāful fund should include both family and general takāful business, unless the family business is only of a short-term nature (risk protection only); IFSB-8 requires separate treatment for provisioning and investment of family and general business (para 129)

Regulatory capital requirements establish a PCR (control level above which the supervisor does not intervene on capital adequacy grounds) and an MCR (breach invokes strongest supervisory actions — the ultimate safety net), with the MCR subject to a minimum bound, e.g. a market-wide nominal floor; a new fund could require initial capitalisation by waqf or qarḍ; the PCR cannot be less than the MCR (Standard XVI, paras 165-169)

PCR and MCR are determined per segregated fund (including the SHF); where capital resources of one fund cannot support another, the PCR and MCR of the TU as a whole may be the sum of the PCRs and MCRs of its constituent funds (paras 176-177)

Example target criteria cited: a 99.5% VaR calibrated confidence level over a one-year horizon (the calibration of the IAIS ICS and European Solvency II), a 99% TVaR over one year (Swiss Solvency Test modelling criteria), and a 95% TVaR over the term of the takāful contract obligations; different criteria apply for PCR and MCR (paras 199, 324, fns 31, 49, 51)

Calibration distinguishes the shock period (period over which a shock is applied) from the effect horizon (period over which the shock impacts the TU); at the end of the shock period capital must be sufficient so that assets cover technical provisions and other liabilities redetermined at that point (paras 200-202)

The supervisor should address at least underwriting risk, credit risk, market risk, operational risk and liquidity risk, including risk concentrations and wrong way risk; Sharī'ah non-compliance risk must be included within operational risk, with non-compliance potentially causing loss of capital resources by refund of contributions or purification of tainted income plus reputational damage (paras 189-191, 195-196)

The IAIS ICS Standard Method is presented as an adaptable illustration: stress-based and factor-based risk charges aggregated with correlation matrices, applied at the level of each segregated fund; takāful adaptations rename insurance risk as takāful risk and premium risk as takāful contribution risk, and avoiding ribā is expected to obviate interest-rate risk directly related to a contract though discount-rate shocks still affect valuations; the ICS has no module for climate change risk, which should be incorporated into standard formulae or addressed via capital add-ons (paras 213-217, Table 1, fn 35, para 216)

Qarḍ provided from the SHF for capital support is potentially reclassifiable as capital resources of the takāful fund only where subordinated to takāful participants' claims (achievable by voluntary and irrevocable agreement of the provider); to prevent double counting and internal leverage it must be excluded or deducted from SHF capital resources, by default against the highest quality of capital in the SHF (paras 234-238)

A qarḍ facility (a voluntary and irrevocable commitment by the TO to transfer earmarked SHF assets to the takāful fund as qarḍ) may be recognised as contingent capital with supervisory approval, provided it can absorb losses, is represented by identified, unencumbered, suitably transferable earmarked assets, is not double-counted in SHF resources, and the TO is legally obliged to transfer on prescribed events including MCR shortfall or winding-up; repayment of qarḍ or release from earmarking should be restricted where it is foreseeable that the fund will fail its PCR (paras 242-245, 285)

Tiering example: a minimum level of 50% of required capital for high-quality capital elements and/or an upper limit of 25% of required regulatory capital for lowest-quality capital; perpetual subordinated loan capital and perpetual cumulative preference share capital may be limited to 50% of required capital; under the ICS, Tier 1 absorbs losses going concern and in winding-up, Tier 2 only in winding-up, and for a mutual the Tier 1 limited plus Tier 2 resources are limited to 60% of the ICS capital requirement — an undrawn qarḍ facility is analogous to non-paid-up capital (paras 303, 314-318)

Where a capital instrument is a Sharī'ah-compliant fixed-income instrument such as a sukuk, the supervisor must consider whether periodic payments by the TO represent redemption of principal, and how to preserve permanence (para 288)

Use of internal models for regulatory capital requires prior supervisory approval and satisfaction of a statistical quality test, a calibration test and a use test, plus documentation standards and ongoing validation; cherry-picking between approaches (e.g. using the model only when it gives a lower requirement) is discouraged, including for partial internal models covering only some funds (Standard XXIV, paras 319-328)

In group-wide capital adequacy assessment (group-level focus or legal entity focus), no diversification benefit should be recognised between segregated funds (or SHF assets earmarked as qarḍ) of TUs in the group and other group members unless the supervisor is satisfied the funds can absorb losses elsewhere; multiple gearing, intra-group creation of capital, reciprocal financing and leverage must be identified and treated to prevent duplicative use of capital (paras 332, 362, 372, 374-377)

standards.applicability: Framework of principles and rules of conduct of business (COB) for Regulatory and Supervisory Authorities (RSAs) supervising takāful undertakings; expands on IFSB-27 CPIFR-Takāful with specific focus on TCP-19 Conduct of Business (para 9). Developed primarily in reference to the hybrid takāful model; provisions are, where relevant (with modifications if required), also applicable to takāful windows and other forms of Islamic insurance qualified as Sharīʻah-compliant by a central Sharīʻah board, government stipulation, or a Sharīʻah board structured in line with international Sharīʻah governance standards (para 10). Minimum requirements to be applied proportionately to the nature, scale, and complexity of TUs (paras 18-19). Detailed COB principles may not be appropriate for retakāful transactions where benefits under a takāful contract are not affected by the retakāful arrangements, though TUs and retakāful providers must still provide each other complete and accurate information (para 20). Implementation may depend on, and is without prejudice to, the general legal framework of the jurisdiction (para 23).

Section 2: Conduct of Business in Takāful — general requirements for COB (paras 24-30); COB supervisory staff (paras 31-32); Sharīʻah compliance assertions (paras 33-37); segregation of funds (paras 38-48); surplus distribution (paras 49-58); responsibilities for COB (paras 59-66); fiduciary duties of TOs (paras 67-70); representation of participants (paras 71-72); managing conflicts of interests (paras 73-80); qarḍ (paras 81-86); intermediaries (paras 87-94). Section 3: Fair Treatment of Consumers — product development and pre-contractual stages, product approval approach, principles-based approach, adequacy of information, disclosure of rights and obligations (paras 95-124); contract servicing, information on the provider, information on terms and conditions (paras 125-140); claims management (paras 141-143); complaint management (paras 144-150). Section 4: Digital Distribution and Products — knowledge about customers through digitalisation, AI and protected groups, behavioural insights and products/pricing, new digital market players (paras 151-186). Section 5: Conduct of Business Risk Oversight and Supervision — COB risk, identification, supervisory tools, assessing risk through the product lifecycle, indicators for COB risks (paras 187-219). Section 6: Consumer Financial Education (paras 220-238). Definitions. Appendix 1: Gap Assessment Matrix.
key_points: The standard is recommended for implementation by RSAs effective from January 2026 onwards, with an adequate pre-implementation period from the issuance date; earlier implementation is encouraged where RSAs are comfortable and able (paras 21-22)

It expands on IFSB-27 CPIFR-Takāful with specific focus on TCP-19 (Conduct of Business), which is closely aligned with the IAIS Insurance Core Principles as adopted in November 2019 but modified for Sharīʻah application; the 2006 IFSB-IAIS paper identified four themes and the IFSB has issued eight takāful/retakāful standards (paras 2-3, 9)

Developed primarily for the hybrid takāful model (two-tier structure hybrid of a mutual and a commercial company); also applicable, with modifications, to takāful windows and other Islamic insurance models; risks are not transferred to the TO but remain with participants, and PRF and PIF must be segregated from SHF (paras 10, 12, fn 1)

Terminology: 'participant' is a person in a takāful arrangement with rights to compensation; 'customer' covers participants of takāful and Islamic insurance schemes; 'applicant' is a potential customer; 'consumer' covers both customer and applicant; 'provider' refers to TU and Islamic insurance undertakings (para 17)

Sharīʻah compliance is the raison d'être of Islamic insurance; supervisors should require a Sharīʻah governance structure, periodic Sharīʻah audit/review reports, and a BOD- and Sharīʻah-board-approved policy on Sharīʻah non-compliance incidents covering steps on identification, disposal of Sharīʻah non-compliant income, and sanctions (paras 33-36)

Segregation of funds requires at minimum an SHF bearing all administrative and management expenses and at least one PRF pooling risk-related contributions and covering all claims and claims-handling costs; PRF investment may be structured as muḍārabah with the TO as muḍārib; the TO charges a wakālah fee to the PRF and the SHF may provide interest-free qarḍ in case of deficit (para 39)

The underwriting surplus has a different legal underpinning (tabarruʿ) than investment profit (muḍārabah): the TO must not share the surplus, and any surplus-related performance or incentive fee, whether fixed or a percentage, is not chargeable to the PRF; the IFSB Sharīʻah board holds this view though practices differ in various jurisdictions (paras 39, 51, fn 11)

TOs must have BOD- and Sharīʻah-board-approved policies for each PRF covering risks covered, trigger events for benefits, attributed expenses, surplus/deficit determination, utilisation of surplus and deficit coverage, and winding-up procedure; consolidation of PRFs may be allowed only with policies covering sustainability, fair treatment, actuarial assessment, and assurance of no outstanding qarḍ (paras 42, 46)

Supervisors should prohibit TOs from distributing surplus if the fund has qarḍ payable — the surplus should first fully pay off the outstanding qarḍ; RSAs may take punitive actions where a TO created unrealistic surplus expectations by representations or actions, and may prohibit distribution when retention is critical for fund viability (paras 53-54)

Surplus utilisation options include: distribution in proportion to contributions net of claims; distribution to all participants irrespective of claims; cash, reduced future contributions, or transfer to PIF; donation for social/charitable purposes; retention in the PRF for solvency; deferred payout on surrender or death claim (similar to reversionary bonus); enhanced benefits; or reserves for events like natural disasters; surplus or deficit may be determined annually (paras 55-58, fn 16)

The wakālah contract creates a fiduciary relationship between participants (principals) and the TO (agent/wakīl); TOs and intermediaries must give participants' interest precedence over their own profit motives, and the TO must disclose the legal quality of its contractual relations (paras 67-69)

To give participants 'a voice', TOs could use a regular participant assembly, online meetings with digital voting, a director for participants' affairs, or a liaison office; RSAs can introduce 'participant advocates' by regulation — independent parties reviewing operations and fair treatment, with costs borne by the participants' fund or split with shareholders (paras 71-72)

Unit-linked family takāful conflicts of interest include biased fund pre-selection, fund-manager fee rebates retained by the TO, and risk-appetite differences between TO (muḍārib) and participants (rab-ul-maal); supervisors should mandate that TOs pass through discounts on third-party investment management fees to reduce expenses charged to the PRF or PIF (paras 78-79)

A wakālah fee calculated as a percentage of gross contributions creates conflict-of-interest risk: higher turnover from poor underwriting benefits TOs but can cause PRF deficits; a worked example shows a 25% wakālah fee on $100 contributions leaving $75 in the PRF against $70 of liabilities, with the $5 surplus distributable but the fee not refunded in proportion, creating an incentive to overcharge (para 80, fn 45)

RSAs may require TOs to provide qarḍ when PRF assets are insufficient to cover liabilities and the required solvency margin, or when the PRF has a liquidity shortage; supervisors should establish trigger points, and may require write-off of qarḍ or (even retroactive) reduction of management fees to a reasonable amount where deficits result from mismanagement or excessive fees; deficits due to TO negligence may require outright transfer of assets from SHF to PRF instead of qarḍ (paras 82-85)

Intermediaries must disclose details of any commission received prior to customer engagement and whether they act exclusively for a single TO or a panel; RSAs may ban specific incentive systems (e.g., volume-based incentives) that can lead to adverse customer outcomes (paras 87, 90)

Product oversight uses a product approval approach and/or a principles-based approach; supervisory approval is more appropriate for less financially capable or vulnerable consumers, new or complex products, or legally required contracts (e.g., automobile liability or health takāful); approval may still be required for first-time innovative features, first-time or changed Sharīʻah contracts, or products requiring at least one new PRF, and RSAs must have powers to prohibit, suspend, amend, or sanction products (paras 105, 107, 112-113)

In family takāful, participants must specify the nominee's role (executor or beneficiary) in written form; entitlements from the PIF should be distributed among the participant's heirs according to Islamic inheritance law, and the death benefit is considered part of the deceased's property distributed under Sharīʻah rules of bequest and inheritance, with the nominee as trustee if nothing else is determined (paras 110, 209, fn 28)

The wakālah fee must be expressed both as an absolute amount per participant and as a percentage of contributions payable, must cover management and distribution expenses plus a reasonable margin of operating profit, and all fees must be certified by the actuary and approved by the Sharīʻah board; participants must know the qarḍ amount to be recovered and the TO's intended recovery time frame and portion of future surpluses used (paras 136-137)

Complaints must first be filed with the provider and only escalated to alternative dispute resolution (ADR) if unresolved in the specified time; for Sharīʻah disputes, eligibility criteria for arbitrators/ombudsmen can include being a Muslim, knowledge and competence in the disputed matters, familiarity with Sharīʻah arbitration procedures, knowledge of the Sharīʻah, and neutrality and impartiality (paras 149-150)

Digital distribution: AI-based underwriting using Big Data can produce algorithmic discrimination against protected groups, so supervisors can require full details of training data, processing methods, and bias tests; to prevent digital cross mis-selling of add-on insurance, sales should be separated, prices displayed per component, components individually (de)selectable, pre-ticked boxes avoided, and distinct cooling-off periods allowed — the UK FCA found less than 20% of premiums for such add-ons paid out in claims (2019 data) (paras 158-159, 168-169, fn 38)

Providers should charge the same rates to customers with the same risk profiles, refrain from pricing by individual likelihood of switching at renewal, and as best practice commit to renewal prices not higher than equivalent new contracts (paras 175-176)

COB risk indicators include commission rates, high wakālah fees (which can prevent qarḍ recovery or force the PRF into deficit), surrender ratio, claims ratio, claims rejected ratio, claims open ratio, combined ratio (below 100% indicates profit; 'lower than normal' may signal poor value for money), GWC growth, new contract growth/ratio, return ratio, ongoing costs, and illiquidity ratios (para 215)

Takāful-specific COB risk indicators: trend of Sharīʻah non-compliant income; pattern of Sharīʻah-compliance disputes; surplus level (unusually high surplus may indicate overcharging or honouring fewer claims); and PRF deficit — continuous deficits and persistent reliance on qarḍ can be against participants' best interest; digital financial education should clarify what a deficit, excessive wakālah fees, and unpaid qarḍ in a PRF mean for participants' value for money (paras 219, 236)
divergence_notes: On conventional reinsurance vs retakāful: "The concept of 'darurah', or necessity in the absence of a compliant alternative, is used by some TUs to justify the use of conventional reinsurance rather than retakāful. Different authorities may hold different opinions as to whether the conditions for darurah are satisfied. The International Islamic Fiqh Academy (IIFA) resolved that Islamic insurance companies should reinsure only with Islamic reinsurance companies except where that is not possible and 'for other valid reasons'" (fn 8, para 46)

On the TO not being entitled to a surplus-related incentive fee: "The IFSB Sharīʻah board holds the view stated above. However, it is worth noting that practices differ in various jurisdictions in this regard" (fn 11, para 51)
Foreign Islamic insurance providers should inform participants of "the process of how the provider manages different opinions between jurisdictions and how it asserts Sharīʻah compliance" (para 130)

On the nominated beneficiary of a death benefit in family takāful: the benefit is distributed among heirs per Sharīʻah rules of bequest and inheritance, but "Some jurisdictions might have a different practice which can be in line with Islamic inheritance law" (para 209, fn 46)

Family takāful benefit distribution: providers should mention, "based on the jurisdiction's preference", the Sharīʻah basis of the distribution of benefits (e.g., Islamic Law of inheritance, bequest); where local law does not facilitate distribution per Islamic inheritance law, the TO can provide benefits to the nominee with an explanation to relieve the TO of Sharīʻah-compliance responsibility (para 110, fn 27)
