Shari'ah non-compliance risk (2.10, paras 211-218); P12 internal audit provides independent assurance to board, SSB and senior management (2.11, paras 219-223); P13 remuneration structure should support sound corporate governance and risk management (2.12, paras 224-235); P14 IIFS shall acknowledge IAH's right to monitor performance of their investments (2.13.1, paras 236-250); P15 sound investment strategy aligned to IAH risk/return expectations, transparent in smoothing (2.13.2, paras 251-260); P16 governance adequately transparent to shareholders, IAH, depositors, stakeholders and market participants (2.14.1, paras 261-269); P17 transparency in Shari'ah governance (2.14.2, paras 270-271); P18 adequate and timely disclosures to IAH and public on investment accounts (2.14.3, paras 272-279); P19 disclosure of Islamic social finance/sustainability impact (2.14.4, paras 280-285); P20 RSAs should provide guidance for and supervise corporate governance (2.15, paras 286-304); P21 RSAs shall have adequate understanding of Shari'ah non-compliance risks (2.15.6, paras 305-307). Then Definitions section; Appendix 1 Gap Assessment Matrix comparing BCBS Guidelines (2015), IFSB-3 and IFSB-10 against the RCG (note: the matrix cites 'Principle 22, paragraph 309-312' although the body contains 21 principles ending at para 307).
key_points: IFSB-3, the first IFSB corporate governance standard, was issued in 2006 and focused on (a) safeguarding the rights of Investment Account Holders (IAH) and (b) ensuring compliance with Shari'ah principles (para 3)

The standard builds upon the BCBS 'Corporate Governance Principles for Banks' (July 2015), amending and enhancing them for Islamic finance specificities and emerging issues incl. climate-related financial risks (CFR), cyber risks and SDGs; the initiative was approved at the 37th IFSB Council Meeting in December 2020 (paras 6-8)
A principle-based approach is used; the Guiding Principles consist of 21 high-level principles taken from the BCBS Guidelines and IFSB-3, with detailed text and recommended practices (paras 23, 29)

Scope: full-fledged Islamic banks, Islamic investment banks/companies, Islamic windows of conventional banks, and other institutions determined by the RSA; digital banks included at RSA discretion (para 30, fn 13)

Minimum requirements applied with flexibility commensurate with maturity, size, complexity, structure, business model, economic significance and risk profile; 'comply or explain' disclosure approach recommended (paras 31-32); supervisory authorities recommended to adopt effective from 1 January 2025 (para 35)
The term 'compliance' throughout includes adherence to Shari'ah rules and principles unless otherwise stated; the board may delegate functions to committees but not its responsibilities (para 36)

Risk governance rests on three lines of defence: business line; independent risk management and compliance functions (second line); and independent internal audit inclusive of internal Shari'ah audit (third line) (paras 18, 55-61)

IIFS shall have an internal Shari'ah compliance unit/department (ISCU), or at least a Shari'ah compliance officer within the compliance team, competent, adequately resourced, and separate and independent from business units (para 60)

RSAs should discourage the CEO also acting as board chairman; the chair should be an independent or non-executive board member, and the board should assess each member's ongoing suitability at least annually (paras 26, 81, 85)

The audit committee is responsible for both financial audit and Shari'ah audit; it should be entirely independent/non-executive members incl. expertise in Shari'ah-compliance audit (preferably well-versed in Fiqh al-Mua'amalat and Usul al-Fiqh), and must coordinate with the SSB and governance committee (paras 97-98, 101)
A risk committee is required for systemically important banks, must have an independent chair, a majority of independent members, and must review the IIFS's risk policies at least annually (para 102)

A compensation committee is required for systemically important banks (paras 108, 225); remuneration for material risk-takers should defer compensation with 'malus/forfeiture' and 'clawback' provisions; 'golden hellos' and 'golden parachutes' are generally not consistent with sound compensation practice (para 233); control-function remuneration determined independently of business lines (para 228)

A governance committee is required for IIFS offering investment accounts; it protects stakeholders other than shareholders (particularly IAH), oversees policies on PER and IRR, fair profit computation and distribution, and IAH rights during liquidation; recommended composition is at least three members (an audit committee member, a member with Shari'ah expertise, and a non-executive director) (paras 92, 109, 112-114)

PER and IRR must be subject to internal and external audits to prevent misuse or unfair treatment favouring shareholders; IIFS cannot use the PER and IRR to pay zakat or IIFS benefits such as administrative expenses (fn 38)

Senior management members are required to have Islamic finance qualifications obtained through formal education, professional certification, formal training, or workshops as determined or recognised by the RSA (paras 137-138)

For Islamic windows, senior management of the conventional bank should appoint a specific senior executive responsible for monitoring and managing the windows; it is strongly recommended this executive be responsible only for Islamic windows and report directly to the CEO (paras 150, 152-153)

In group structures the subsidiary board should adjust group policies where they conflict with an applicable Shari'ah ruling; the conventional parent's representatives on the Islamic subsidiary's board should abstain from voting on RSA-determined issues that could benefit the parent at the expense of the subsidiary's stakeholders (paras 158, 162)

The CRO must be independent with no 'dual hatting' (COO, CFO, chief auditor or other senior manager should not also serve as CRO); appointment, dismissal and changes to the CRO position should be board/risk-committee approved and publicly disclosed (paras 180-181)

IFSB-1 requires comprehensive risk management processes for six risks: credit risk, equity investment risk, market risk, liquidity risk, rate of return risk, and operational risk; operational risk includes reputational risk from Shari'ah non-compliance (paras 198-199)

Under mudarabah, the IAH as rabb al-mal bears the risk of losing invested capital while the IIFS as mudarib (understood as both management and shareholders) owes a fiduciary duty to IAH no less than to shareholders; shareholders and IAH rank pari passu as residual claimants in commingled asset pools (paras 237-239, fn 69)

Where investment accounts are managed under wakalah the IIFS earns a flat fee plus possible performance-based incentives; RSAs should use stringent eligibility criteria for including wakalah- or musharakah-based accounts in the definition of investment accounts (paras 241-242)

Smoothing IAH returns via the PER raises transparency and accountability concerns; IIFS must inform IAH whenever profits are transferred to or drawn from reserves, must distinguish the 'distribution rate' from the 'profit rate', and the PER shall not be used to compensate for loss in capital — the IRR serves that purpose (paras 253, 256, 258-260)

On liquidation, IAH bear loss only in proportion to assets funded by their investments; the IIFS is liable for losses from its own negligence, misconduct or breach of investment mandate; both PER and IRR are included in a constructive or actual liquidation (para 249, fn 73)

Minimum annual disclosures include board recruitment approach, SSB selection criteria, committee meetings and SSB meetings with attendance (para 263); Shari'ah governance disclosures must include an SSB compliance statement, accessible rulings with justifications, departures from rulings, and the amount and type of Shari'ah non-compliant income and its discharge (para 271); IIFS offering Islamic social finance (zakah, sadaqah, waqf) shall disclose impact per IFSB-22 Section 10 (paras 280, 284); RSAs must allow Shari'ah-compliant services, including Islamic windows, only by licensed IIFS (para 305)
divergence_notes: 'IFSB recognises different opinions and practices in Shari`ah rulings across jurisdictions. Hence, RSAs should refer to relevant Shari`ah authority in their respective jurisdictions' (fn 10); the document 'is not to be understood as approving any specific Shari'ah ruling or fatwa of any kind' (para 22)

'There are potentially different Shari'ah requirements within regulatory frameworks across jurisdictions' — e.g. different Shari'ah requirements between the parent company's and subsidiary's jurisdictions, different types of IIFS with different SSBs in a group, or different SSBs in each IIFS; internal documentation should be shared with the parent's SSB (para 159, fns 51-52)
The subsidiary board should make necessary adjustments 'where a group policy conflicts with an applicable Shari'ah ruling' (para 158)

'the Shari'ah governance system may vary across jurisdictions and there is no "one-size fits all" approach in designing a Shari'ah governance framework' (para 132); the IFSB 'recognises Shari'ah governance models employed by different jurisdictions that vary in terms of their unique organs of Shari'ah governance' (para 28)

Interpretation of Islamic ethical values is at the discretion of RSAs and/or IIFS in consultation with relevant Shari'ah authority/scholars, considering primary sources, international standards and universal ethical values incl. local tradition or custom ('urf) (fn 23)

standards.applicability: Cross-sectoral: banks, insurance companies, non-bank financial institutions (e.g. asset managers) and issuers in Islamic capital markets; for non-financial issuers only the Shariah governance of their compliant securities and issuance processes (para 8 + fn 1); proportionality by size/complexity of the jurisdiction's Islamic financial system (para 12).
standards.structure: 15 principles in Section 2: P1 Supervisory Expectations; P2 Board and Senior Management; P3 Shariah Governance Framework; P4 Risk Management; P5 Disclosure and Transparency; P6 Islamic Windows; P7 Group Structures; P8 Outsourced Activities; P9 Screening; P10 Corrective Actions; P11 Issuers of Shariah-compliant Securities; P12 Supervisory Approach; P13 Enforcement and Remedial Action; P14 Supervisory Resources and Capacity; P15 Cooperation and Information-sharing.
key_points: Supervisory oversight of Shariah governance is integral to financial stability and consumer protection mandates — it 'does not necessarily involve the assessment or issuance of Shariah-compliance rulings by the supervisor' (para 1).
Complements IFSB-10; excludes general corporate governance covered by IFSB-30 (paras 2, 7).
Recommended supervisor implementation by January 2027 (para 15).

Definitions distinguish Central Shariah Authority (established within a regulatory/supervisory body) from National Shariah Authority (established by national legislation/government, independent of the supervisor) (fn 4).
Where supervisors have limited/no Shariah-governance mandate, they can implement key aspects via consumer-protection and market-integrity mandates (disclosure + market conduct supervision) (para 11).
Centralised institutional arrangements must themselves be subject to a governance framework like IIFS Shariah boards: independence, resources, member competence, conflict mitigation (para 19).
Board bears ultimate responsibility for Shariah governance; approves framework, conflict-of-interest policies, ensures organs have authority, independence, resources (paras 22-23).
Board collectively needs sufficient Islamic-finance knowledge; continuous professional development policies (paras 24, 27).

External Shariah audit: Board approves appointment/removal/remuneration and monitors auditor independence and effectiveness (para 31); external Shariah auditor must report directly to the supervisor on findings of material significance (para 47).
Organs of Shariah governance typically: Shariah board, Shariah compliance function, Shariah risk management, internal Shariah audit, sometimes external Shariah audit (fn 9).
Supervisors must counter selective pursuit of favourable rulings ('fatwa shopping' risk): document ruling processes, disclose rationale behind each ruling (para 37).
IIFS must submit Shariah board members' affiliations, external appointments and remuneration structure to the supervisor for independence assessment (para 38).
Where an IIFS-level Shariah board exists, its rulings must be BINDING and mandatory on the IIFS (para 41).
Three lines of defence: business line; Shariah compliance + risk management; internal Shariah audit — the latter organisationally distinct and barred from second-line work (para 41 + fn 13).
Escalation: structured process for Shariah non-compliance incidents to senior management/board; early mitigation expected (para 50).

Disclosure: ALL Shariah non-compliance events reported to the supervisor 'irrespective of materiality'; public disclosure of events with and without financial implications, incl. procedural lapses, nature, impact, corrective actions (para 52).
Sector disclosure anchors: IFSB-22 (banking), IFSB-25 (takaful), IFSB-19 and IFSB-21 (capital markets) (para 54).

Islamic windows (banking + takaful): Principle 3 requirements apply with proportionality; qualified senior executive with Islamic-finance expertise appointed to manage the window, with defined roles and resources (paras 55-57).

Groups: conventional parent board oversight of Islamic subsidiaries; at least one parent board member knowledgeable in Islamic finance encouraged where activities significant (para 58); subsidiary boards assess compatibility of group Shariah policies with local requirements (para 61).
Outsourcing: full IIFS accountability retained; outsourced Shariah advisory must be independent of the firm doing external Shariah audit; providers meet fit-and-proper criteria (paras 63-64).

Screening: criteria endorsed by own Shariah board OR external list/methodology endorsed by a qualified Shariah authority; periodic review; annual-report statement from Shariah advisors plus external Shariah auditor report where applicable (paras 67-68).

Corrective actions: divestment procedures for non-compliant assets; purification payments with conflict-of-interest safeguards (paras 69-70; fn 2 defines corrective action as rectification incl. divestment/purification).

Issuers: Shariah approval mechanisms pre- and post-issuance (esp. on asset changes, enforcement, restructuring); corrective policies if a security is later found non-compliant; host-jurisdiction compliance for foreign offerors (paras 71-75).

Supervisory approach: regular comprehensive assessments (reports, minutes, interviews, on/off-site); more frequent for systemically important IIFS (para 77); supervisors may consult a national/central Shariah authority or recognised body when exercising judgment (para 79).
Where central/national pronouncements are binding, supervisors ensure institutional alignment, with escalation/clarification mechanisms back to the issuing authority (para 81).

Enforcement: remedial timetables, escalation, sanctions proportionate to risk; for issuers — corrective disclosures, restrictions on future issuances, possible reclassification of an instrument's compliance status (paras 83-86).
divergence_notes: Jurisdiction models diverge: legal frameworks granting explicit supervisory powers vs market-driven approaches leaving Shariah governance to IIFS and market forces (para 9).
Institutional approaches vary: centralised bodies (central Shariah authority at supervisor level, or national Shariah authority) vs Shariah boards only at IIFS level (para 18).
'In some jurisdictions, central or national Shariah authorities are advisory in nature, whereas, in others, pronouncements issued by such authorities are considered binding' (fn 6).
Significant differences in legislative/regulatory frameworks may require legal change or modification of principles per jurisdiction (para 5).
